name: Chinto (Wado-ryu)
meaning: Named, per established folklore, after the stranded Chinese sailor Chinto whose fighting methods Matsumura recorded; Otsuka kept the Okinawan name where Funakoshi had substituted Gankaku.
era: Wado version 1930s (declared among the nine official kata, 1977)
origin_person: attributed to Sokon Matsumura (folklore); Wado adaptation by Hironori Otsuka
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (created); Hironori Otsuka (standardised)
provenance: Otsuka's Chinto keeps the straight-line embusen and crane stances but re-engineers the form around Wado principles of evasion and body-shifting rather than Shotokan's deep power line, making it the most advanced of the nine official Wado kata. Otsuka declared it among the nine official kata in 1977. THE ROW THE CLIENT FLAGGED. It carried the single id wado-ryu while every sibling Wado row carried three or four. Added wado-kai, wado-kokusai, wado-ryu-karate-do-renmei, shintani-wado-kai. Chinto is one of Otsuka's nine declared official kata and is a WKF shitei kata for Wado-ryu, so it is universal across every Wado body. CANONICAL FORM: 'Chinto' (the existing tomari-te row, which already lists wado-ryu).

provenance: Funakoshi's Japanese rename of the Tomari kata Wanshu, traditionally (folklore) traced to the 1683 Chinese sapposhi Wang Ji. The Shotokan version follows the Itosu line of the kata and was further polished during the 1930s-40s reforms associated with Gigo Funakoshi. Renamer: Gichin Funakoshi, Karate-dō Kyōhan (1935). Wholly new characters: 燕飛, 'flight of the swallow', named for the rising and dropping in the form, replacing the personal name Wanshu. The Shotokan line descends from Itosu's Wanshu, not from Kyan's. Gigo's revision supplied the long stances and the driving rear leg; the JKA fixed the competition tempo. DATA FIX: rows 52 (Empi) and 53 (Enpi) are the same kata entered twice with conflicting eras (1935 against 1936) and different style lists. provenance: The core of the roughly dozen kata Asai created for his JKS curriculum after leaving the JKA, designed to reintroduce whipping, one-legged and rotational actions he felt standard Shotokan had lost; they are now examined kata within JKS worldwide. (Note: Junro is Asai Shotokan, not an Ashihara or Enshin form.) The Junro series (Shodan to Godan) is a Tetsuhiko Asai creation and the row already credits him, but its styles field carries only shotokan, whereas every other Asai kata in the file (Joko, Kakuyoku, Kashu, Kibaken, Kyakusen, Meikyo Sho, Rakuyo, Roppo, Seiryu, Sensho, Shotei, Suishu, Hachimon, Hyakuhachiho, Gankaku Sho) carries asai-ryu|japanese-karate-generic|shotokan. Proposing the same three ids for consistency. I have not proposed a modifier value, since I found no source naming one for Junro specifically. Explicitly remedial/foundation kata, not part of the dan repertoire. Carr

name: Kihon Kumite (Wado-ryu)
variants: Kihon Kumite Ipponme-Jupponme; Yakusoku Kumite kata
meaning: 'Fundamental paired forms': ten prearranged two-person sequences that Otsuka regarded as kata in their own right, encoding Wado's core principles of nagasu (flowing), inasu (evading) and noru (riding) an attack.
introduced_by: Hironori Otsuka (created)
provenance: Otsuka fused Shindo Yoshin-ryu jujutsu pairwork with karate striking to create these paired kata, the most distinctive Japanese-created element of the Wado syllabus and the clearest expression of the style's jujutsu inheritance. They sit alongside, not below, the solo kata in Wado pedagogy. Otsuka's paired forms carrying the Shindo Yoshin-ryu content of Wado. Carried the bare id wado-ryu. Added wado-kai, wado-kokusai, wado-ryu-karate-do-renmei, shintani-wado-kai. The ten Kihon Kumite are universal across Wado bodies (Otsuka left them unstandardised, so the sequences differ between organisations, but all teach them). NOT flagged disputed: the parenthetical is doing real work here because 'Kihon Kumite' unqualified would collide with generic basic sparring drills in other styles.

name: Sochin (Shotokan)
variants: Hakko (Funakoshi's proposed rename, not adopted); Sochin
renamed_from: Sōchin (壮鎮) of the Aragaki line: Funakoshi's substitute name Hakkō ('eight storms') did not survive
meaning: 'Tranquil strength' or 'preserve the peace': strength held in stillness, expressed through the rooted sochin-dachi (fudo-dachi), the 'immovable stance' that dominates the kata.
origin_person: Yoshitaka (Gigo) Funakoshi, reworking the Aragaki-line Sochin
modified_era: late 1930s to early 1940s, before Gigo's death on 24 November 1945
introduced_by: Gigo Funakoshi (created)
provenance: The Shotokan Sochin differs so extensively from Aragaki Seisho's Naha/Tomari Sochin (kept in Shito-ryu) that it is treated as Gigo Funakoshi's creation, exemplifying his deep-stance, powerful reform of Shotokan. Gichin Funakoshi's proposed Japanese rename Hakko never displaced the old name. The clearest single example of the distinction the client wants. Gichin attempted the renaming, to Hakkō, and it failed; Gigo did the technical work, and it stuck. Gigo brought the Aragaki-line Sōchin into Shotokan while studying Shitō-ryū material, and rebuilt the whole kata on fudō-dachi, the rooted stance now called sōchin-dachi after it, in place of the Shitō-ryū nekoashi-dachi and zenkutsu-dachi. The result is close to a new kata sharing an embusen with its parent. Record Gichin as attempted renamer (name rejected) and Gigo as modifier, not as creator, since the source kata is Aragaki's. name: Tekki
meaning: 'Iron horseman' or 'iron horse riding': named for the kata's rooted horse-riding stance (kiba-dachi), and, by Nakayama's account, in homage to the power of Funakoshi's teacher Itosu, who shaped the form.

provenance: Funakoshi's Japanese rename of Naihanchi, the sideways-fighting kata he himself spent roughly ten years studying under Azato and Itosu. The lateral straight-line embusen and kiba-dachi were retained; the three-part division (Shodan to Sandan) follows Itosu's late Okinawan arrangement. Renamer: Gichin Funakoshi, Karate-dō Kyōhan (1935). Unlike Heian, this is a wholly new name in new characters: 鉄騎, 'iron horse' or 'iron cavalry', replacing the untranslatable Okinawan Naihanchi. What changed: the Okinawan naihanchi-dachi, a shoulder-width stance with the toes turned in, was widened into the long, low kiba-dachi (cavalry-horse stance); Funakoshi is recorded using the term kiba-dachi for this posture by 1936. provenance: Shotokan's shortest kata, generally attributed to Gigo Funakoshi as an unfinished reworking of the Tomari Wankan; it entered the standard JKA syllabus after the war. None displaced Wankan in general use. provenance: Guarelli's account: Chikin Shosoku Oyakata, condemned to death for factional fighting in Shuri, was exiled to Tsuken-jima instead because of his renown as a bo expert; there he lodged with a fisherman named Akachu ('red man', from his sun-darkened complexion), taught him bojutsu, and was surpassed by him. Akachu then created an oar kata for defence against sword, lance and staff, sharpening the oar's edge (name-giri). The Matayoshi school received the eku from two sources: the Matayoshi family, in which it was Matayoshi Shinchin's favourite weapon, and Chokuho Agena.

meaning: 'Maezato's nunchaku'. Maezato was Taira Shinken's birth surname (he took his mother's name Taira later), so the kata is self-named: his own codification of the horse-bridle flail into a formal kata.
introduced_by: Shinken Taira (created)
provenance: Little classical nunchaku kata survived into the 20th century; Taira composed this form (and Maezato no Tekko) under his birth name to fill the gap in his 1955 Ryukyu Kobudo syllabus.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taira_Shinken | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunchaku | https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B9%B3%E4%BF%A1%E8%B3%A2

name: Maezato no Tekko
variants: Maezato no Tecchu (distinct weapon); Maezato nu Tekko; Tekko
meaning: 'Maezato's iron knuckles'
introduced_by: Shinken Taira (created); Eisuke Akamine (standardised)
provenance: Composed by Taira Shinken under his birth surname; transmitted through the Ryukyu Kobudo Hozon Shinkokai.
sources: Taira Shinken, Ryukyu Kobudo Taikan (1964) — not verified in corpus

name: Manji no Sai
meaning: 'swastika/manji sai', from the reversed-prong implement
introduced_by: Shinken Taira (created); Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Eisuke Akamine (standardised)
provenance: Composed by Taira Shinken for the manji-sai; the implement itself was introduced to Okinawa by Shinko Matayoshi, who copied it from a weapon seen in Shanghai.
sources: Taira Shinken, Ryukyu Kobudo Taikan (1964) — not verified in corpus

name: Matayoshi no Nunchaku
variants: Matayoshi nu Nunchaku; Nunchaku (Matayoshi); Nunchaku Dai Ichi; Nunchaku Dai San
meaning: 'Matayoshi's nunchaku'

introduced_by: Irei Okina (created); Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (standardised); Shinko Matayoshi (created)
provenance: Guarelli: 'The nunchaku techniques also come from Okina Irei... The Matayoshi no nunchaku kata is sometimes called as Nunchaku dai san. In all likelihood, it was taught, with minimum variations, in the 1960s.'

name: Matayoshi no Sai
variants: Nicho Sai; Sai Dai Ichi; Sai Dai Ni; Sancho Sai; Sancho Sai (三丁釵); Shinbaru no Sai
meaning: 'Matayoshi sai'. The graded sai kata of the Matayoshi curriculum (dai ichi and dai ni, plus the three-sai form Sancho Sai in which a third sai is carried for throwing), blending Okinawan saijutsu with Chinese methods from the Kingai-ryu inheritance.
origin_place: Naha, Okinawa (with Chinese elements from Fuzhou)
introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (created); Shinpo Matayoshi (standardised); Shinpo Matayoshi (created)
provenance: An informal umbrella name used by practitioners for the Matayoshi sai kata.
sources: https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1908088 | https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1908090 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sai_(weapon)

name: Matayoshi no Tunkua
variants: Matayoshi no Tonfa; Matayoshi no Tonfa Dai Ichi; Matayoshi no Tonfa Dai Ni; Tunkua Ichi/Ni; Tunkuwa Dai Ichi; Tunkuwa Dai Ni; Tunkuwa Ni Dan
meaning: 'Matayoshi tonfa' (tunkua is the Okinawan name of the millstone-handle weapon). The paired kata dai ichi and dai ni codify the Matayoshi family's tonfa method, marked by circular flywheel strikes and simultaneous double-arm actions.
introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (created); Shinpo Matayoshi (standardised); Irei Okina (created)
provenance: Umbrella name for the three Kodokan tonfa kata.
sources: https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1908088 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonfa | https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1908090

name: Nicho Sai
variants: Matayoshi no Sai Dai Ichi (deprecated); Nichosai
meaning: 'two sai'
era: c. 1920s (Guarelli: created by Shinpo Matayoshi 'after the First World War')
modified_era: 1960s-1970s (codification for the Zen Okinawa Kobudo Renmei)
introduced_by: Shinpo Matayoshi (created)
provenance: Created by Shinpo Matayoshi as a training form on the sai basics taught to Shinko Matayoshi by Chokuho Agena. Now the first sai kata of the Matayoshi syllabus.

name: Nunchaku Dai Ni
meaning: 'second nunchaku form'
introduced_by: Andrea Guarelli (created)
provenance: Created by Guarelli within the Matayoshi tradition for the A.I.K.O. and later IMKA syllabus, alongside a Nunchaku kiso kata for beginners and two prearranged nunchaku-versus-bo sets.

name: Nunti
variants: Nunti Bo; Nunti no Kata; Nuntibo
meaning: 'Nunti' (a six-foot staff mounted with a manji-shaped sai head, derived from a fishing gaff). The kata codifies thrusting, hooking and trapping methods unique to this fisherman's weapon, with paired manji sai often thrown or held in the belt.
introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (created); Shinpo Matayoshi (standardised)
provenance: The nunti is emblematic of the Matayoshi school's preservation of fishing- and farming-implement arts; Shinko gathered the methods during his travels and Shinpo fixed the kata for the Zen Okinawa Kobudo Renmei.
sources: https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1908088 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okinawan_kobud%C5%8D | https://okic.okinawa/en/

name: Nunti Bo no Kata

meaning: 'form of the piercing staff'
era: techniques learned by Shinko Matayoshi c. 1930-1934 in China; kata codified mid 20th century

origin_place: Fuzhou and Shanghai, China; codified in Naha
introduced_by: Kingai (Jin Ying) (created); Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (standardised)
provenance: Guarelli: 'Master Shinko Matayoshi learned the nunti-jutsu art from an old Chinese master Jin Ying (Kingai) in Shangai (China)'; nunti-bo handling is close to the bo methods of Tsuken Island. Only one kata exists in the school.

introduced_by: Eisuke Akamine (created)

meaning: 'Three-section staff, number one'. Kata for the Chinese sanjiegun, three staves linked by cord or chain; its presence in Okinawan kobudo comes from Matayoshi Shinko's training in Fuzhou under the monk Kingai.

modifier: An unnamed student of Shinpo Matayoshi, who composed it

name: Tinbe (Matayoshi)
meaning: 'Shield (and short spear)'. The Matayoshi line's tinbe-rochin kata, using a turtle-shell shield and short hooked spear; its low, evasive circling is attributed to the Chinese methods Matayoshi Shinko absorbed in Fuzhou.
origin_place: Naha, Okinawa; Chinese elements from Fuzhou
introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (standardised)
provenance: Part of the material linked to Shinko's studies with the monk Kingai in Fuzhou (the Kingai-ryu inheritance); fixed for public teaching by Shinpo Matayoshi. Added matayoshi-kobudo-imka and matayoshi-kodokan, to match the sibling row. CANONICAL FORM: 'Tinbe nu Ti' (ティンベーぬ手), which the file already holds with exactly this id set. The two rows are the same Matayoshi tinbe form under a shortened name.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinbe-rochin | https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1908088 | https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1908090

name: Tinbe nu Ti
variants: Matayoshi no Tinbe; Tinbe no Te; Tinbe-Rochin (Matayoshi)
meaning: 'shield techniques'
era: composed mid 20th century; Chinese source techniques learned by Shinko Matayoshi c. 1930-1934
origin_person: Shinpo Matayoshi (composition); Kingai / Jin Ying (technical source)
origin_place: Naha, Okinawa; techniques from Fuzhou, Fujian
introduced_by: Kingai (Jin Ying) (created); Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (created)
provenance: Guarelli: 'The kata Tinbe nu ti or Matayoshi no tinbe was composed by Shinpo Matayoshi based on the techniques he learned from his father. However it is told that this form has been influenced also by tinbe techniques of the Ryukyu Kobu-jutsu.' The underlying tinbe-jutsu is Kingai-ryu, learned by Shinko Matayoshi from the Chinese master Kingai (Jin Ying).

name: Bassai
variants: Bal Sae; Bassai Dai; Pal Che; Palsek; Passai; Patsai
meaning: 'To extract from (or storm) a fortress': the name evokes breaking through an enemy stronghold, reflected in the kata's driving, penetrating techniques.
era: Passai 18th-19th century; in Korea from mid-1940s
origin_person: Attributed variously to Sokon Matsumura and Oyadomari lineages (origin uncertain)
origin_place: Shuri/Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
modifier: Hwang Kee (Moo Duk Kwan); Lee Won-kuk (Chung Do Kwan)
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (standardised); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (brought); Byung Jick Ro (brought)
provenance: The Korean form follows Itosu's Passai Dai as transmitted in Shotokan (Bassai Dai); it is the signature mid-dan hyung of Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do and appears as Pal Che or Palsek in kwan-era taekwondo syllabi. Attribution of the original Passai is contested Okinawan tradition rather than documented fact. Korean recension of Passai and the gateway form to black belt. CORRECTION. The existing 'attributed variously to Sokon Matsumura and Oyadomari lineages (origin uncertain)' imports Okinawan uncertainty that does not apply to the Korean transmission, which is short and reasonably clear. Two routes, both from the Japanese redaction: Hwang Kee worked from Japanese-language books on Okinawan karate in the Chosun Railway Bureau library in Seoul between 1939 and 1945, never identifying the titles though internal evidence points to Funakoshi; and Lee Won-kuk of the Chung Do Kwan trained directly
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passai | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do

name: Bigak
meaning: 'Flying kick'. Competition poomsae for competitors aged 18 to 30; the most athletically demanding of the set. Also romanised Bikkak.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.

name: Chil Sung Chil Ro
meaning: 'Seven star, seventh path'. The final and most advanced form of the series.

name: Chil Sung Il Ro
meaning: 'Seven star, first path'. Chil Sung refers to the seven stars of the Big Dipper in Ursa Major, an object of Korean folk veneration; the series is Hwang Kee's attempt to give Moo Duk Kwan a Korean rather than Okinawan form vocabulary.
modified_era: Revised after 1957, once Hwang Kee obtained the Muye Dobo Tongji; codified in his 1978 manual
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Original composition. Hwang Kee stated the movements draw on the Muye Dobo Tongji (1790) and on the 'Joong Gan Ryu' or middle-way principle of soft, flowing motion, in deliberate contrast to the linear Japanese kata.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Soo Bahk Do Institute, Chil Sung Hyung Series | Wasatch Martial Arts, 'Background of Chil Sung Hyung'

meaning: 'Seven star, fourth path'.

name: Chil Sung series
variants: Chil Sung Il Ro to Chil Ro; Chil Sung hyung
meaning: 'Seven stars', referring to the Big Dipper (seven-star constellation), symbolising guidance and the connection of the practitioner to the cosmos; seven forms blending hard karate-derived technique with soft, breath-led Chinese-style movement.
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Hwang Kee's own creation, drawing on his study of northern Chinese arts and Yang-style-influenced soft movement, designed to express his philosophy of Neh Gung (internal) and Weh Gung (external) energy; they became the signature hyung of Soo Bahk Do Moo Duk Kwan. Hwang Kee's own compositions, distinct from the Okinawan-derived hyung.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwang_Kee | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soo_Bahk_Do

name: Choi-Yong
meaning: Named for General Choi Yong, premier and commander-in-chief of the armed forces during the 14th century Koryo dynasty, revered for loyalty, patriotism and humility; he was executed by his subordinate commander Yi Sung-gye, who went on to found the Yi dynasty. 46 movements.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Chon-Ji
meaning: 'Heaven and Earth'; interpreted as the creation of the world and the beginning of human history, hence the first pattern taught. 19 movements, in two parts (heaven, earth).
modified_era: Standardised in the 1965 Taekwon-Do textbook and again in the 1983 Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Newly composed at the Oh Do Kwan / 29th Infantry Division; no Okinawan kata antecedent, but its technical vocabulary (walking stance, low block, middle punch) is Shotokan by way of Chung Do Kwan.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Taekwon-Do (1965); Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | ITF pioneers page, itftkd.sport

name: Chonkwon
meaning: 'Heaven's great mandate' or 'sky fist'. Heaven as the infinite and mysterious source of creation, worshipped from antiquity; the movements are large and circular to express its boundlessness.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Seventh dan poomsae.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kukkiwon Textbook

provenance: Original ATA composition.

name: Choong Jung Il Jang

name: Choong-Jang
meaning: Pen name of General Kim Duk-ryang, who lived during the Yi dynasty in the 14th century. 52 movements. The pattern ends with a left-hand attack to symbolise the tragedy of his death in prison at the age of 27, before he could reach full maturity.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Choong-Moo
meaning: Chungmu was the posthumous title given to Admiral Yi Sun-sin (1545-1598), credited with the kobukson (turtle ship) of 1592, held to be the first armoured battleship. 30 movements. The pattern ends with a left-hand attack to symbolise his regrettable death before he could show his unrestrained loyalty to the king.
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Dan-Gun
meaning: Named for Dangun Wanggeom, the legendary founder of Korea in 2333 BC. 21 movements; all blocks and strikes are performed high, said to symbolise Dangun climbing the mountain.

introduced_by: Park Jung-tae (created)
provenance: Original GTF composition in the Chang Hon idiom.
sources: GTF syllabus, taekwondo.global

name: Do-San
meaning: Pen name of Ahn Chang-ho (1876-1938), independence activist and educator who promoted Korean education and the independence movement in the United States. 24 movements represent his 24 years of dedication.
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983)

name: Eoullim
meaning: 'Harmony' or 'coming together'. Competition poomsae for competitors in their 30s and 40s.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

name: Eui-Am
meaning: Pen name of Son Byong-hi, leader of the Korean independence movement of 1 March 1919. 45 movements refer to his age when he changed the name of Dong Hak to Chondo Kyo (Heavenly Way religion) in 1905; the diagram signifies his indomitable spirit displayed while dedicating himself to the prosperity of his nation.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Ge-Baek
meaning: Named for Gye Baek, the Baekje general who led 5,000 men against a far larger Silla-Tang force at Hwangsanbeol in 660 AD. 44 movements; the diagram signifies his severe and strict military discipline.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Hansol
meaning: 'Great pine'. Competition poomsae for competitors in their 50s and 60s.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

name: Hansu
meaning: 'Water', the source of all life, adaptable and inexhaustible. The performance line traces the hanja 水 (water).
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Eighth dan poomsae.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: Himchari
meaning: 'Powerful challenge'. A competition poomsae for tournament competitors under 18.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed for the final rounds of poomsae competition, to give judges greater technical discrimination between elite performers. No historical antecedent.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016 | Taekwondo Wiki, Kukkiwon Competition Poomsae

name: Hwa Sun
meaning: 'Flowering' or 'flower of goodness'. The name echoes Hwa Soo Do ('flowering hand way'), the original 1945 name of Hwang Kee's art before he adopted Tang Soo Do.
era: Late in Hwang Kee's career; usually dated to the 1980s, occasionally to the 1970s
modifier: Hwang Kee; subsequently transmitted by H.C. Hwang
modified_era: Promulgated through the Soo Bahk Do Moo Duk Kwan Federation in the 1980s and 1990s
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created); Hwang Hyun-chul (H.C. Hwang) (transmitted)
provenance: Original composition, the last hyung Hwang Kee created, again claimed as a Muye Dobo Tongji derivation. Taught only at senior dan grades in Soo Bahk Do.
sources: Hwang Kee, Soo Bahk Do Volume 2 | Soo Bahk Do Moo Duk Kwan Federation syllabus | Wikipedia, 'Soo Bahk Do'

name: Hwa-Rang
meaning: Named for the Hwarang, the youth corps of the Silla dynasty around 600 AD. 29 movements refer to the 29th Infantry Division, where taekwondo was developed into maturity under Choi and Nam Tae-hi.
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition; the 29th Division reference makes it effectively the Oh Do Kwan's signature pattern.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015) | Bok Man Kim entry, Taekwondo Wiki

name: Ilyeo
meaning: 'Oneness', the Buddhist doctrine of the unity of body and mind, matter and spirit, taught by the Silla monk Wonhyo (617-686). The performance line traces the manja 卍, the Buddhist swastika.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Ninth dan poomsae, the highest in the Kukkiwon canon. Honours the same monk as the ITF pattern Won-Hyo.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: In Wha Ee Jang
meaning: 'Harmony between people', second level. Seventh ATA colour-belt form.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: In Wha Il Jang
meaning: 'Harmony between people', first level. Sixth of the nine ATA colour-belt forms.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: Jee-Goo
meaning: 'The earth' or globe, signifying the worldwide reach intended for the federation.
introduced_by: Park Jung-tae (created)
provenance: Original GTF composition.
sources: GTF syllabus, taekwondo.global

name: Jee-Sang
meaning: 'Above the earth'. Jee is the earth, the foundation of the world; sang is that which stands above it, taken to represent the spirit of the GTF. 24 movements for the 24 hours of each day.
era: c. 1990, on the founding of the Global Taekwon-Do Federation
introduced_by: Park Jung-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition in the Chang Hon idiom, added by Park Jung-tae after he broke with Choi Hong-hi over the Juche pattern and other matters. GTF practises the ITF patterns plus six of Park's own.
sources: GTF syllabus, taekwondo.global | Taekwondo Wiki, Global Taekwondo Federation

name: Jin Do
meaning: Korean reading of Chintō, traditionally the name of a shipwrecked Chinese sailor whose fighting method Sokon Matsumura codified; Funakoshi's rename Gankaku ('crane on a rock') describes its one-legged crane stances.
era: Chintō mid-19th century; in Korea from mid-1940s
origin_person: Attributed to Sokon Matsumura, from the sailor Chintō (folklore)
origin_place: Tomari/Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (created); Hwang Kee (brought); Won Kuk Lee (brought)
provenance: The Tang Soo Do version follows the Itosu/Shito-ryu-line Chinto pattern more than Shotokan's Gankaku, reflecting the mixed Japanese sources of the kwans; the Chintō shipwreck story is Okinawan folklore. A senior dan hyung in Moo Duk Kwan. Korean recension of Chinto.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinto | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do

name: Jitae
meaning: 'Earth', from ji (earth) and tae (to tread). It represents a man standing on the earth, looking up at the sky, with the earth as the source of life. The performance line traces the hanja for earth-standing man.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Sixth dan poomsae.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: Jook-Am
meaning: 'Bamboo rock', Park Jung-tae's own pen name, chosen on the model of Choi Hong-hi's 'Chang Hon' (blue cottage).
introduced_by: Park Jung-tae (created)
provenance: Original GTF composition. Its use of the founder's own pen name mirrors Choi's naming of the whole Chang Hon system.
sources: GTF syllabus, taekwondo.global

name: Joong-Gun
meaning: Named for An Jung-geun, who assassinated Ito Hirobumi, first Japanese Resident-General of Korea, at Harbin in 1909. 32 movements represent his age when executed at Lushun (Port Arthur) prison in 1910.
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983)

name: Juche
meaning: Juche is the North Korean philosophical doctrine that man is the master of everything and decides everything, that is, man is the master of the world and of his own destiny. 45 movements; the diagram represents Mount Baekdu.
era: c. 1986; replaced Ko-Dang in the official 24
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the ITF technical committee
modifier: Choi Hong-hi; ITF technical committee (Rhee Ki-ha, Park Jung-tae)
modified_era: 1986, replacing Ko-Dang in the canon of 24
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Park Jung-tae (created); Rhee Ki-ha (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition, created after Choi relocated ITF headquarters and opened relations with the DPRK.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1985 supplement) | Park Jung-tae / GTF founding documents, 1990 | ITF branch syllabi

name: Jung Yul
meaning: 'Righteous discipline' or right rhythm. Second-degree black belt form; 82 movements.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: Keumgang
meaning: 'Diamond', from the Buddhist Vajra, meaning that which is hard and indestructible. Named for Mount Kumgang, the most celebrated mountain in Korea, and for the Keumgang Yeoksa, the guardian warriors carved at temple gates. The performance line traces the hanja 山 (mountain).
era: Created 1965-1967 with the Palgwae; adopted 1967 and retained after 1972
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Second dan poomsae. Unlike the Palgwae, the yudanja set survived the 1972 revision.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo' | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: Kicho Hyung
variants: Ki Cho Hyung Il Bu / E Bu / Sam Bu; Kibon; Kicho
meaning: 'Foundation forms'. Three elementary I-pattern forms teaching low block, middle punch and stance turning; the Korean counterpart of the Shotokan Taikyoku series.
origin_person: Gichin Funakoshi and Gigo Funakoshi (Taikyoku model); adapted by Hwang Kee and Won Kuk Lee
origin_place: Tokyo, Japan; adapted in Seoul, Korea
introduced_by: Gichin Funakoshi (created); Hwang Kee (standardised); Won Kuk Lee (brought)
provenance: Modelled on the Taikyoku kata of Shotokan, which the kwan founders learned in Japan or from Funakoshi's books; Hwang Kee formalised them as Ki Cho Hyung Il Bu, E Bu and Sam Bu in the Moo Duk Kwan. Most kwans used equivalents as first-geup forms before the Pyung Ahn series. Basic series taught before the Pyung Ahn.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taikyoku | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do

name: Kicho Hyung Ee Bu
meaning: 'Basic form, part two'. As part one but with the punches delivered at high level.
era: Modelled on Taikyoku Nidan; Korean version from the mid-1940s
origin_person: Gichin and Gigo Funakoshi (model); adapted by Hwang Kee
introduced_by: Gichin Funakoshi (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (modified)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Taikyoku Nidan, brought across by Won Kuk Lee from Funakoshi's Shotokan and adopted in parallel by Hwang Kee.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Kidokwan, 'Quest for the Truth'

name: Kicho Hyung Il Bu
meaning: 'Basic form, part one'. A teaching form of front stance, low block and lunge punch on the I-shaped embusen.
era: Modelled on Taikyoku (c. 1936-1940); Korean version taught from the mid-1940s
origin_person: Gichin Funakoshi and Gigo Funakoshi (Taikyoku Shodan model); Korean version adapted by Hwang Kee
modified_era: Late 1940s to 1950s, fixed in Hwang Kee's 1958 and 1978 manuals
introduced_by: Gichin Funakoshi (created); Gigo Funakoshi (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (modified)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Taikyoku Shodan. Carried across by Won Kuk Lee, who trained under Funakoshi at Shotokan in Tokyo, and independently adopted by Hwang Kee from Funakoshi's published texts.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Gichin Funakoshi, Karate-do Kyohan | Kidokwan, 'Quest for the Truth: The Origin of Tang Soo Do's Forms'

name: Kicho Hyung Sam Bu
meaning: 'Basic form, part three'. Introduces the back stance and inside-outside block.
era: Modelled on Taikyoku Sandan; Korean version from the mid-1940s
origin_person: Gichin and Gigo Funakoshi (model); adapted by Hwang Kee
introduced_by: Gichin Funakoshi (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (modified)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Taikyoku Sandan, via the same double route.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Kidokwan, 'Quest for the Truth'

name: Ko-Dang
meaning: Pen name of the patriot Cho Man-sik (1883-1950), who devoted his life to the independence movement and the education of his people. 39 movements represent his times of imprisonment and his birthplace on the 39th parallel.
era: 1962-1964, Malaysia period; removed from the official 24 c. 1986
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
modifier: Choi Hong-hi (removed it); Park Jung-tae (restored it in the GTF, 1990)
modified_era: Removed 1986; restored by the GTF from 1990
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Park Jung-tae (transmitted)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition; still taught in GTF and in several ITF splinter federations.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | GTF syllabus, taekwondo.global | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Kong Sang Koon
variants: Kanku Dai; Kong Sahng Koon; Kong Sang Kun; Kusanku; Kushanku
meaning: The Korean reading of the Chinese characters 公相君 (Kusanku), the honorific title of a Chinese envoy to Okinawa c. 1756 whose fighting method inspired the kata; the Koreans preserved the older personal name rather than Funakoshi's rename Kanku ('viewing the sky').
era: Kata c. 1760s-1800s; in Korea from mid-1940s
origin_person: Kata attributed to Tode Sakugawa, after the envoy Kusanku
origin_place: Okinawa (Chinese influence via Fuzhou); brought to Seoul, Korea
introduced_by: Kusanku (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: Transmitted to Korea as Shotokan's Kanku Dai but retained under its Okinawan name in Korean reading; it is the longest and most senior of the classical Tang Soo Do hyung. The story of the envoy Kusanku teaching his art is early tradition recorded in the Oshima Hikki (1762). Korean recension of Kusanku.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kusanku | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do

name: Koryo
meaning: The Goryeo dynasty (918-1392) and the seonbae spirit of the scholar-warrior who resisted the Mongols. The performance line traces the hanja 士 (seonbi, 'scholar'), signifying the learned man of conviction.
modified_era: 1975 onwards; details clarified in successive Kukkiwon Textbook editions
introduced_by: Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created); Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created)
provenance: Original composition. First dan poomsae; note it replaced a same-named 1967 form of entirely different content.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo' | jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020)

name: Kwang-Gae
meaning: Named for Gwanggaeto the Great, 19th king of Goguryeo, who recovered the lost territories including most of Manchuria. 39 movements refer to the first two figures of 391 AD, the year he took the throne; the diagram represents the expansion and recovery of lost territory.
era: 1962-1964, while Choi was ambassador to Malaysia
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
modified_era: Published 1965; revised with sine-wave in the 1983 Encyclopedia
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition, worked out in Kuala Lumpur during Choi's ambassadorship.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015) | ITF pioneers page, itftkd.sport

name: Moon-Moo
meaning: Named for King Munmu, 30th monarch of the Silla dynasty. 61 movements refer to the last two figures of 661 AD, the year he came to the throne. His body was buried near Dae Wang Am (Great King's Rock) after he asked, in his will, that his body be placed in the sea so that his spirit might for ever defend Korea against Japanese aggression.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Narae
meaning: 'Wings'. Competition poomsae for competitors in their 50s and 60s.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

name: Nareusya
meaning: 'Flying upward', from the archaic Korean of the Yongbieocheonga. Competition poomsae for competitors aged 18 to 30.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae, kicking-intensive.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

name: O Sip Sa Bo
variants: Gojushiho; Oh Sip Sa Bo; Useishi
meaning: 'Fifty-four steps': direct Korean reading of Gojushiho (五十四歩), the number 54 having Buddhist significance (half of 108); the kata's flowing, drunken-crane movements are among the most advanced in the Shuri-te canon.
origin_person: Shuri-te transmission via Sokon Matsumura and Anko Itosu
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (standardised); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: The highest classical karate-derived hyung in Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do/Soo Bahk Do, deriving from Useishi/Gojushiho of the Matsumura-Itosu line as transmitted in Japanese karate. Korean recension of Gojushiho, taught at 4th dan and above.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gojushiho | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do

name: Old Koryo (Koryo Il Jang)
meaning: 'Koryo' names the Goryeo dynasty (918-1392), from which the Western name 'Korea' derives, and the seonbae warrior-scholar spirit that repelled the Mongol invasions.
era: Created 1965-1967; adopted 1967; superseded by the new Koryo in 1972
modifier: Superseded, not modified: the 1971-72 committee wrote an entirely new Koryo rather than revise this one
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition, companion to the Palgwae series. Survives in Jung Do Kwan and other conservative lineages and in some overseas Chung Do Kwan schools; largely extinct in mainstream Kukki taekwondo.
sources: 'The Original Koryo Hyung Part 1', jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Onnuri
meaning: 'The whole world'. Competition poomsae for competitors in their 50s and 60s.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016 | Taekwondo Wiki, 'Bikkak and Hanryu'

name: Palgwae Chil Jang
meaning: Trigram Gan (간, ☶), mountain. Ponderousness and stability; movement halted with finality.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Palgwae Ee Jang
meaning: Trigram Tae (태, ☱), joyfulness, the lake. Firmness within, softness without; movements should be performed with inner calm and confidence.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition, Shotokan-derived vocabulary.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Palgwae Il Jang
meaning: Trigram Keon (건, ☰), heaven and light, the pure yang. As the origin of all things it is the first and most basic of the set.
era: Developed 1965-1967; adopted by the KTA 1967; superseded 1972
origin_person: Korea Taekwondo Association poomsae committee (1965-67), chaired collectively by five kwans
modifier: Retained unchanged by the ITF-independent Kukkiwon dissenters; never revised by the KTA, which replaced rather than amended the series
modified_era: Frozen in 1967; replaced by Taegeuk Il Jang in 1972
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Newly composed for the unified KTA curriculum, drawing on Shotokan-derived Chung Do Kwan and Song Moo Kwan basics. No Okinawan kata antecedent.
sources: 'The Original Koryo Hyung Part 1', jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo' | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: Palgwae Oh Jang
meaning: Trigram Seon (손, ☴), wind. Both gentle and destructive; humility and penetrating persistence.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Palgwae Pal Jang
meaning: Trigram Gon (곤, ☷), earth, the pure yin. Receptivity and the nurturing ground on which everything takes root; the last of the gup-grade set, immediately before black belt.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Palgwae Sa Jang
meaning: Trigram Jin (진, ☳), thunder. Great power and dignity; danger met with courage.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Palgwae Sam Jang
meaning: Trigram Ri (리, ☲), fire and the sun. Warmth, enthusiasm and hope.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Palgwae Yuk Jang
meaning: Trigram Gam (감, ☵), water. Ceaseless flow; hardship overcome by constancy.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Palgwae series
variants: Palgue; Palgwae Il Jang to Pal Jang
meaning: 'Eight trigrams' (palgwae = bagua): eight forms keyed to the eight trigrams of the I Ching, from Keon (heaven) to Gon (earth), representing the full range of natural phenomena.
introduced_by: Lee Chong-woo (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created)
provenance: The KTA's first unified coloured-belt set, drafted by a committee drawn from a subset of kwans (including Lee Chong-woo of Jidokwan and Lee Kyo-yoon of Hanmookwan, with Kwak Kun-sik, Hyun Jong-myun, Park Hae-man, Kim Soon-bae and others); because major kwans were unrepresented, an expanded committee replaced the set with the Taegeuk poomsae in 1971-1972, though many schools still teach Palgwae. Colour-belt curriculum of the early KTA.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyeong | https://www.kukkiwon.or.kr

name: Po-Eun
meaning: Pen name of Chong Mong-chu (1400), a loyalist poet and physicist of the Koryo dynasty, remembered for the line 'I would not serve a second master though I might be crucified a hundred times'. 36 movements; performed entirely along a straight line to symbolise unswerving loyalty.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Pyong-Hwa
meaning: 'Peace', the aspiration for reconciliation on the Korean peninsula, standing in the GTF canon roughly where Tong-Il stands in the ITF's.
introduced_by: Park Jung-tae (created)
provenance: Original GTF composition.
sources: GTF syllabus, taekwondo.global

name: Pyongwon
meaning: 'Plain' or open plateau, the vast fertile land that sustains human life. The performance line traces the hanja 一, the single horizontal stroke of the plain.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Fourth dan poomsae.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: Pyung Ahn Cho Dan
native: 평안 초단 / 平安 初段
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence, first level'. Corresponds to Pinan Nidan in the Okinawan order (Itosu's second form), which Funakoshi reversed with Shodan; Tang Soo Do follows the Shotokan Heian order.
era: Pinan created c. 1904-1907; in Korea from the mid-1940s
modifier: Hwang Kee, Won Kuk Lee and Byung Jick Ro (Korean renderings)
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Byung Jick Ro (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Pinan Shodan / Heian Shodan. Carried to Korea by Won Kuk Lee (from Funakoshi, Tokyo), Byung Jick Ro (also from Funakoshi, Tokyo) and adopted by Hwang Kee at Moo Duk Kwan.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C | Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Gichin Funakoshi, Karate-do Kyohan

name: Pyung Ahn Ee Dan
native: 평안 이단 / 平安 二段
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence, second level'. Corresponds to Pinan Shodan in the Okinawan order.
era: Pinan c. 1904-1907; in Korea from the mid-1940s
modifier: Hwang Kee, Won Kuk Lee, Byung Jick Ro
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Byung Jick Ro (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Pinan Nidan / Heian Nidan, brought across by Won Kuk Lee and Byung Jick Ro from Funakoshi's Shotokan.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C | Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

name: Pyung Ahn O Dan
native: 평안 오단 / 平安 五段
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence, fifth level'. The final and technically densest of the set.
era: Pinan c. 1904-1907; in Korea from the mid-1940s
modifier: Hwang Kee, Won Kuk Lee, Byung Jick Ro
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Byung Jick Ro (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Pinan Godan / Heian Godan.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C | Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

name: Pyung Ahn Sa Dan
native: 평안 사단 / 平安 四段
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence, fourth level'.
era: Pinan c. 1904-1907; in Korea from the mid-1940s
modifier: Hwang Kee, Won Kuk Lee, Byung Jick Ro
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Byung Jick Ro (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Pinan Yondan / Heian Yondan.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C | Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

name: Pyung Ahn Sam Dan
native: 평안 삼단 / 平安 三段
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence, third level'.
era: Pinan c. 1904-1907; in Korea from the mid-1940s
modifier: Hwang Kee, Won Kuk Lee, Byung Jick Ro
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Byung Jick Ro (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Pinan Sandan / Heian Sandan.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C | Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

name: Pyung Ahn series
variants: Heian; Pinan; Pyong An; Pyung Ahn Cho Dan to Oh Dan; Pyung An
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence' or 'safety and calm': the Korean reading of Pinan (平安), Itosu's name expressing that mastery of the five forms lets one defend oneself with a calm mind.
era: Created c. 1904-1907; in Korea from mid-1940s
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Byung Jick Ro (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: Itosu's five Pinan (drawn largely from Kusanku and Channan) reached Korea as Shotokan's Heian through Won Kuk Lee (Chung Do Kwan) and Byung Jick Ro (Song Moo Kwan), both Funakoshi students, while Hwang Kee learned them substantially from Japanese karate books; Yun Kwae-byung's Ji Do Kwan transmitted Shudokan/Shito-ryu versions. They remain the core geup forms of Tang Soo Do and early taekwondo. Korean recension of Itosu's Pinan series.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinan | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do

name: Saeara
meaning: 'New sea' or new ocean. Competition poomsae for competitors in their 30s and 40s.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

name: Saebyeol
meaning: 'New star'. Competition poomsae for competitors aged 18 to 30.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

name: Saju Jirugi / Saju Makgi
meaning: 'Four-direction punch' and 'four-direction block': pre-pattern fundamental exercises teaching turning, blocking and punching to the four compass points before the student learns Chon-Ji.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and early Oh Do Kwan instructors
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Introductory exercises of the Chang Hon system, codified in Choi Hong-hi's Taekwon-Do texts and the 1983 Encyclopedia; not counted among the 24 tul. Four-direction punch and block exercises, the ITF entry point.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyeong | https://taekwondo.fandom.com/wiki/Saju_Jirugi

name: Saju Tulgi
meaning: 'Four-direction thrust'. A pre-pattern exercise drilling the straight fingertip thrust and guarding block in four directions, taught alongside Saju Jirugi (four-direction punch) and Saju Makgi (four-direction block).
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi and early Oh Do Kwan instructors
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon teaching exercise, modelled on the four-direction basic drills common to Shotokan-derived Korean kwans. Not counted among the 24 tul.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983), volume on fundamental exercises | ITF and GTF gup syllabi

name: Sam-Il
meaning: 'Three-one', denoting 1 March 1919, the date of the Korean independence movement. 33 movements represent the 33 patriots who planned it.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Se-Jong
meaning: Named for King Sejong the Great, who invented the Korean alphabet in 1443 and was a noted meteorologist. 24 movements represent the 24 letters of the Korean alphabet; the diagram represents the character for 'king'.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Sei Shan
meaning: 'Thirteen', usually explained as thirteen hands, thirteen techniques or thirteen postures. In Korean Shotokan-derived lineages also called Ban Wal ('half moon'), after Funakoshi's Hangetsu.
era: Seisan 17th-19th century; in Korea from the mid-1940s
origin_person: Origin unknown; among the oldest kata in the Okinawan repertoire, of Fujian Chinese derivation
origin_place: Naha and Shuri, Okinawa; ultimately Fujian
introduced_by: Gichin Funakoshi (renamed); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Seisan by way of Funakoshi's Hangetsu. Brought to Korea by Won Kuk Lee and Byung Jick Ro from Tokyo; taught by Hwang Kee in the Moo Duk Kwan dan syllabus.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C | Gichin Funakoshi, Karate-do Kyohan | Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

name: Shim Jun
meaning: 'Reaching a level of purity of mind'. First-degree black belt form; 81 movements, that is 9 x 9.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition. The nine black-belt forms culminate in the ninth-degree form of 99 movements.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: Sip Soo
meaning: 'Ten hands': the Korean reading of Jitte (十手), traditionally meaning one who masters the kata fights with the strength of ten men.
era: Jitte 19th century; in Korea from mid-1940s
origin_person: Unknown; Tomari-te kata standardised through Itosu
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (standardised); Hwang Kee (brought); Won Kuk Lee (brought)
provenance: Derives from the Tomari-te kata Jitte as codified in Shotokan; in Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do it is a dan-grade hyung noted for its slow, heavy pressing techniques and bo-defence interpretations. Korean recension of Jitte.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_kata

name: Sipjin
meaning: 'Decimal', from the ten sipjangsaeng or symbols of longevity: sun, moon, mountain, water, stone, pine, herb of eternal youth, tortoise, deer and crane. The performance line traces the hanja 十 (ten).
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Fifth dan poomsae; the most technically eclectic of the set, with several movements resembling Okinawan Naha-te shapes.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | comparative kata analyses in taekwondo historiography

name: So-San
meaning: Pen name of the great monk Choi Hyong-ung (1520-1604) of the Yi dynasty. 72 movements refer to his age when he organised a corps of monk soldiers with the help of his pupil Sa Myung Dang, and helped repel the Japanese pirates who overran most of the peninsula in 1592.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Songahm Ee Jang
meaning: Second of the Songahm colour-belt forms; 23 movements.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: Songahm Il Jang
meaning: 'Pine tree, rock', signifying evergreen strength on an immovable foundation. 18 movements, that is 2 x 9, nine being the significant number in the Songahm system (nine colour-belt grades, nine dan grades).
era: 1983 (Songahm forms introduced); system completed through the 1990s
modifier: ATA technical committee under H.U. Lee
modified_era: Refined through the 1980s and 1990s; the full 18-form system settled by c. 1997
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original composition, written expressly to replace the karate-derived Chang Hon and Palgwae forms then taught in the ATA with a set presented as purely Korean. No Okinawan antecedent.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials | ATA / Engage Martial Arts, 'Songahm Star & ATA Forms'

name: Songahm Oh Jang
meaning: Fifth and last of the numbered Songahm colour-belt forms; 34 movements.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: Songahm Sa Jang
meaning: Fourth of the Songahm colour-belt forms; 31 movements.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: Songahm Sam Jang
meaning: Third of the Songahm colour-belt forms; 28 movements.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: Original ATA composition.
sources: ATA Songahm Taekwondo curriculum materials

name: Songahm series
variants: Choong Jung 1-2; Chung San; In Wha 1-2; Jung Yul; Shim Jun; Songahm 1-5
meaning: 'Pine tree and rock': evergreen strength and unbreakable stability, the pen name concept of ATA founder Haeng Ung Lee; a proprietary set of coloured-belt forms (Songahm 1-5, In Wha 1-2, Choong Jung 1-2) and black-belt forms (Shim Jun onwards) designed so each rank's form uses only that rank's techniques.
introduced_by: Haeng Ung Lee (created)
provenance: The American Taekwondo Association replaced its earlier Chang Hon patterns with Haeng Ung Lee's Songahm system from 1983, one of the largest bespoke forms curricula outside the ITF and Kukkiwon canons; practised only within ATA/Songahm-affiliated bodies. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATA_Martial_Arts | https://www.atamartialarts.com

name: Sun-Duk
meaning: Named for Queen Seondeok of Silla (reigned 632-647), the first reigning queen of Korea; the only GTF or ITF pattern honouring a woman.
introduced_by: Park Jung-tae (created)
provenance: Original GTF composition.
sources: GTF syllabus, taekwondo.global | Taekwondo Wiki, Sun-Duk

name: Taebaek
meaning: 'Bright mountain', an ancient name for Mount Baekdu, where Dangun is said to have founded the Korean nation in 2333 BC. The performance line traces the hanja 工, signifying the link between heaven and earth made by man.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created)
provenance: Original KTA composition. Third dan poomsae.
sources: jungdokwan-taekwondo.blogspot.com (2020) | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: Taegeuk Chil Jang
meaning: Trigram Gan (간, ☶), mountain. Ponderousness and immovability; movements must stop cleanly and not be rushed. Introduces the tiger stance, scissor block and knee strike.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Chil Jang.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Taegeuk Ee Jang
meaning: Trigram Tae (태, ☱), joyfulness and the lake. Inner firmness with outward softness; the poomsae should be performed serenely and with a smile.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Ee Jang.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Taegeuk Il Jang
meaning: Trigram Keon (건, ☰), heaven and light, the pure yang and the source of creation. The first and most elementary poomsae.
origin_person: Korea Taekwondo Association poomsae committee (1971-72), the 1965-67 committee enlarged by Ji Do Kwan and Moo Duk Kwan representatives
modified_era: Kukkiwon Textbook editions from 1975; technical clarifications 1987, 2006 and later
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Hyun Jong-myun (created); Lee Yong-sup (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition, replacing Palgwae Il Jang. Technically simpler and more linear than the Palgwae it displaced.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo' | Wikipedia, 'Taegeuk (taekwondo)'

name: Taegeuk Oh Jang
meaning: Trigram Seon (손, ☴), wind. Wind is gentle but can become a hurricane; the poomsae alternates mild and forceful movements, introducing the elbow strike and hammerfist.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Oh Jang.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Taegeuk Pal Jang
meaning: Trigram Gon (곤, ☷), earth, the pure yin. The receptive ground in which everything takes root and from which it grows. The final gup-grade poomsae before first dan.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Pal Jang.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Taegeuk Sa Jang
meaning: Trigram Jin (진, ☳), thunder. Great power and dignity; thunder brings fear but is followed by calm, so the practitioner meets danger bravely.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Sa Jang.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Taegeuk Sam Jang
meaning: Trigram Ri (리, ☲), fire and the sun. Fire gives warmth, energy and hope; the poomsae introduces the knifehand strike and the alternating rhythm of heat and restraint.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Sam Jang.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Taegeuk Yuk Jang
meaning: Trigram Gam (감, ☵), water. Water flows ceaselessly and adapts to any vessel; hardship is overcome by continuity. Introduces the roundhouse kick and outward palm block.
introduced_by: Kwak Kun-sik (created); Park Hae-man (created); Lee Kyo-yoon (created); Kim Soon-bae (created); Lee Chong-woo (created); Bae Young-ki (created); Han Young-tae (created)
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Yuk Jang.
sources: Kukkiwon Textbook | Kidokwan, 'A Modern History of Taekwondo'

name: Toi-Gye
meaning: Pen name of Yi Hwang (1501-1570), authority on Neo-Confucianism. 37 movements refer to his birthplace on the 37th parallel; the diagram represents the character for 'scholar'.
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983)

name: Tong-Il
meaning: 'Unification', denoting the resolution to reunify Korea, divided since 1945. 56 movements; the diagram symbolises the homogeneous race.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition; the final and most demanding pattern of the 24.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: U-Nam
meaning: Pen name of Syngman Rhee, first president of the Republic of Korea. 42 movements.
modified_era: Dropped from all subsequent editions after Rhee's fall in the April Revolution of 1960
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Published in Choi's 1959 Korean-language Taekwon-Do textbook and then erased from the canon. Some ITF historians hold that its movements were recycled into Ko-Dang or Juche.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Taekwon-Do (Korean edition, 1959) | ITF historical reconstructions

name: Ul-Ji
meaning: Named for General Ulji Mundok, who in 612 AD defeated a Tang (Sui) invading force of nearly one million with fewer than 10,000 men, using guerrilla tactics. 42 movements represent Choi Hong-hi's age when he designed the pattern; the diagram represents his surname.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with his pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition. The 42-movement count dates the design precisely to c. 1960 given Choi's 1918 birth, which sits awkwardly with the 1962-64 Malaysia grouping.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Wang Shu
meaning: The Tang Soo Do name for Wanshu, after the Chinese envoy Wang Ji (Sappushi to Ryukyu, 1683), traditionally said to have demonstrated the form in Tomari. Known in Shotokan-derived Korean lineages as Empi or Yun Bi ('flying swallow').
era: Wanshu tradition 17th-19th century; in Korea from the mid-1940s
origin_person: Traditionally the Chinese envoy Wang Ji; actual composer unknown
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora and Chotoku Kyan (Okinawan versions); Gichin Funakoshi (Empi); Hwang Kee (Korean version)
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (transmitted); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed); Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: DERIVES FROM Wanshu / Empi. Brought to Korea by Won Kuk Lee and Byung Jick Ro from Shotokan and adopted by Hwang Kee for the Moo Duk Kwan dan syllabus.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C | Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Shoshin Nagamine, The Essence of Okinawan Karate-do

name: Won-Hyo
meaning: Named for the monk Wonhyo (617-686), who popularised Buddhism in the Silla dynasty in 686 AD. 28 movements.
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition. The same monk is honoured by the Kukkiwon poomsae Ilyeo, whose diagram is the Buddhist manja.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kukkiwon Textbook

name: Yamang
meaning: 'Ambition'. Competition poomsae for competitors under 18.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
introduced_by: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published) (created)
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

name: Yon-Gae
meaning: Named for Yon Gaesomun, the Goguryeo general who repelled the Tang invasion. 49 movements refer to the last two figures of 649 AD, the year he forced the Tang dynasty to quit Korea after destroying nearly 300,000 troops at Ansi Sung.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Yoo-Sin
meaning: Named for General Kim Yu-sin, commanding general of the Silla dynasty. 68 movements refer to the last two figures of 668 AD, the year Korea was unified. The ready posture signifies a sword drawn to the right rather than the left, symbolising Kim's mistake of following the orders of his king to fight his own nation.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Kim Bok-man (created); Woo Jae-lim (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983) | Kim Bok Man, Practical Taekwondo (2015)

name: Yuk Ro Cho Dan (Du Mun)
native: 육로 초단 두문 / 六路 初段 斗門
meaning: 'Six paths, first level: Du Mun', the Great Gate. Yuk Ro means the six-fold path or six roads.
modified_era: Codified in his 1978 manual and in Soo Bahk Do Moo Duk Kwan Federation materials from 1976
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Original composition derived by Hwang Kee from the Muye Dobo Tongji (1790), the Korean royal military manual he obtained in 1957. The text does not fully describe the sequences; Hwang Kee expanded its illustrations into complete forms.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Muye Dobo Tongji (1790) | Capital Soo Bahk Do Academy, 'Yuk Ro Hyung Philosophy'

name: Yuk Ro Ee Dan (Joong Jyel)
native: 육로 이단 중절 / 六路 二段 中節
meaning: 'Six paths, second level: Joong Jyel', to cut the middle. Also romanised Joong Jol.
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Muye Dobo Tongji (1790)

name: Yuk Ro Oh Dan (Sal Chu)
native: 육로 오단 살추 / 六路 五段 殺捶
meaning: 'Six paths, fifth level: Sal Chu', the killing hammer.
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Muye Dobo Tongji (1790)

name: Yuk Ro Sa Dan (Yang Pyun)
native: 육로 사단 양편 / 六路 四段 揚鞭
meaning: 'Six paths, fourth level: Yang Pyun', the high whip.
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Muye Dobo Tongji (1790)

name: Yuk Ro Sam Dan (Po Wol)
native: 육로 삼단 포월 / 六路 三段 抱月
meaning: 'Six paths, third level: Po Wol', to embrace the moon.
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Muye Dobo Tongji (1790)

name: Yuk Ro Yuk Dan (Choong Ro)
native: 육로 육단 충로 / 六路 六段 衝路
meaning: 'Six paths, sixth level: Choong Ro', to seize and capture. The final form of the series.
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978 | Muye Dobo Tongji (1790)

name: Yuk Ro series
variants: Choong Ro; Du Mun; Jung Jul; Po Wol; Sal Chu; Yang Pyun; Yuk Ro Cho Dan to Yuk Dan
meaning: 'Six paths' or 'six-road' forms: six hyung (Du Mun, Jung Jul, Po Wol, Yang Pyun, Sal Chu, Choong Ro), each named for its governing concept, reconstructing indigenous-Korean-flavoured movement from classical texts.
era: Created from 1958, after Hwang Kee's 1957 discovery of the Muye Dobo Tongji
introduced_by: Hwang Kee (created)
provenance: Created by Hwang Kee following his study of the Muye Dobo Tongji (1790 Korean military manual) found in the Seoul National University library in 1957; intended to root Soo Bahk Do in Korean rather than Japanese sources. The forms are modern creations inspired by the text, not reconstructions of surviving ancient forms. Hwang Kee's reconstruction from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soo_Bahk_Do | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muye_Dobo_Tongji

name: Yul-Gok
meaning: Pen name of Yi I (1536-1584), the Neo-Confucian scholar called 'the Confucius of Korea'. 38 movements refer to his birthplace on the 38th parallel; the diagram represents the character for 'scholar'.
introduced_by: Choi Hong-hi (created); Nam Tae-hi (created)
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.
sources: Choi Hong-hi, Encyclopedia of Taekwon-Do (1983)

name: Yun Bi
variants: Empi; Enpi; Eun Bi; Wang Shu; Wanshu
meaning: 'Flight of the swallow', from the darting, rising and dropping movements; the alternate Korean name Wang Shu preserves the older Okinawan title Wanshu, said to honour the Chinese envoy Wang Ji (1683).
era: Wanshu 17th-19th century tradition; in Korea from mid-1940s
origin_person: Traditionally linked to the envoy Wang Ji; Tomari-te transmission
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
introduced_by: Won Kuk Lee (brought); Hwang Kee (brought)
provenance: Reached Korea as Shotokan's Enpi (Funakoshi's rename of Wanshu); Tang Soo Do lineages use both Yun Bi and Wang Shu for essentially the same hyung. The Wang Ji origin story is tradition, not documented history. Korean recension of Enpi/Wanshu.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanshu | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Soo_Do

name: Ashihara kata series
variants: Jissen no Kata; Kihon no Kata 1-3; Kumite no Kata 1-5; Nage no Kata; Shoshinsha no Kata 1-3
meaning: Series names are functional Japanese: beginner's forms, basic forms, sparring forms, throwing forms and real-fight forms; together they encode Sabaki, the repositioning method of moving off-line to the opponent's blind side.
era: 1980s (style founded 1980; kata published in Fighting Karate, 1985)
introduced_by: Hideyuki Ashihara (created)
provenance: Ashihara discarded the traditional Okinawan-Japanese kata canon of his Kyokushin upbringing entirely and composed these modern series so that every movement maps directly onto full-contact fighting at short, middle and long range, performable solo or with a partner. They are documented as kata by the style's own organisations and publications.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashihara_Karate | https://www.ashiharakarate.org/kata/kata-guide/ | https://blackbeltwiki.com/ashihara-katas

name: Enshin kata series
variants: Enshin Kata 1 (white/blue); Enshin Kata 2 (yellow/green); Enshin Kata 3 (brown/black); Nage no Kata
meaning: Named by grade rather than image: graded sequences expressing Enshin's circle-centre (enshin) principle, using Sabaki to convert an opponent's force by moving to the blind spot and unbalancing.
introduced_by: Joko Ninomiya (created)
provenance: Ninomiya, Ashihara's former student, built Enshin's belt-graded kata on the same Sabaki logic as the Ashihara series rather than on classical forms; no kata named Junro is documented in Enshin (that name belongs to Tetsuhiko Asai's Shotokan series). The forms are documented in Enshin organisational material and style references.

name: Pinan sono ichi-go
variants: Heian; Pinan; Pinan sono ichi/ni/san/yon/go; Pinan ura
meaning: 'Peaceful and safe, numbers one to five': Kyokushin retains Itosu's original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's rename Heian.
origin_person: Anko Itosu (originals); Kyokushin adaptation by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; adapted in Tokyo, Japan
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Mas Oyama (standardised)
provenance: Oyama restructured the five Pinan with Kyokushin stances, circular blocks and Goju flavouring, and added ura versions performed with spinning turns, credited to him as a training method for balance and close fighting. The retention of the name Pinan signals Kyokushin's dual Shotokan-Goju parentage. Kyokushin's recension of the Heian/Pinan series. Added iko-1, ifk-kyokushin, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai. Kyokushin's rendering of the Itosu Pinan; universal across the kata-retaining Kyokushin bodies.

name: Sanchin (Kyokushin)
meaning: 'Three battles': the struggle to unify mind, body and technique (or mind, body and spirit) through tension, rooted stepping and ibuki breathing.
era: Qing-era China and Meiji Okinawa; in Kyokushin from the 1950s
origin_person: Fujian Chinese lineage via Kanryo Higaonna; closed-fist version by Chojun Miyagi; brought into Kyokushin by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Fuzhou, China / Naha, Okinawa; Kyokushin version Tokyo, Japan
introduced_by: Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Mas Oyama (brought)
provenance: Oyama absorbed Sanchin through his Goju-ryu training under So Nei Chu (of the Gogen Yamaguchi line) and made it Kyokushin's core conditioning kata, following Miyagi's closed-fist form. The same Goju channel supplied Kyokushin's Gekisai, Saiha (Saifa), Seienchin, Seipai and Tensho. Kyokushin adopted Sanchin from Goju-ryu but places it later than the Okinawan schools do. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan. CANONICAL FORM: 'Sanchin'. One of five 三戦 rows in the file; Oyama's version descends from the Goju line through So Nei Chu and Yamaguchi Gogen and belongs on the canonical entry as a variant.
