name: Sushiho
meaning: 'Fifty-four steps': an alternative Japanese reading of the same characters as Gojushiho, the number 54 carrying Buddhist significance (half of 108, the number of worldly desires).
origin_person: Shuri-te lineage (Matsumura/Itosu line); Kyokushin version by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; adapted in Tokyo, Japan
introduced_by: Mas Oyama (renamed)
provenance: Oyama's rendering of Gojushiho (the old Useshi), reached via its Shotokan transmission and modified to Kyokushin body mechanics; the reading Sushiho distinguishes it from Shotokan's Gojushiho Dai and Sho. It sits among the highest kata of the Kyokushin canon. Kyokushin recension of Gojushiho; the longest kata in the Kyokushin canon. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan, world-oyama. CANONICAL FORM: 'Gojushiho'. Sushiho is the Kyokushin reading of 五十四歩, the fifth row in the file for that kata.
sources: http://the-martial-way.com/history-of-kyokushin-kata/ | https://www.karatephilosophy.com/a-complete-list-of-kyokushin-kata-with-videos/ | https://kyokushin.fandom.com/wiki/Kata

name: Taikyoku sono ichi-san
variants: Sokugi Taikyoku sono ichi-san; Taikyoku sono ichi; Taikyoku sono ni; Taikyoku sono san
meaning: 'Grand ultimate, numbers one to three': the Kyokushin rendering of Funakoshi's Taikyoku, taught as the gateway to the style's kata canon.
origin_person: adapted by Mas Oyama from the Shotokan Taikyoku of Gichin and Gigo Funakoshi
introduced_by: Gichin Funakoshi (created); Gigo Funakoshi (created); Mas Oyama (standardised)
provenance: Oyama, a direct student of Funakoshi, carried the Taikyoku into Kyokushin with modified stances and fighting emphasis, later adding ura (spinning) versions and the Sokugi (kicking) Taikyoku set unique to the Kyokushin lineage. They remain the first kata across nearly all Kyokushin offshoots. Kyokushin inherited the Taikyoku set from Shotokan as its beginner curriculum. Added iko-1, ifk-kyokushin, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai. The Kyokushin rows split into two inconsistent tagging habits: some carried the IKO/IFK set, others the Kyokushin-kan/Seido/World Oyama/Shidokan set, for kata that are in every one of those syllabi. Ashihara, Enshin, Seidokaikan, Byakuren and Zendokai are deliberately excluded throughout: those offshoots dropped the classical kata for their own sets, which the file already records separately.
sources: https://www.karatephilosophy.com/a-complete-list-of-kyokushin-kata-with-videos/ | https://uskyokushin.com/kyokushin-kata | https://blackbeltwiki.com/kyokushin-katas

modifier: Kyokushinkaikan honbu instructors; syllabus fixed by the IKO

name: Tensho (Kyokushin)
meaning: 'Rotating palms' (or 'revolving hands'): soft circular open-hand movements over a Sanchin base, the yin counterpart to Sanchin's hardness.
origin_person: Chojun Miyagi (created 1921, drawing on the Chinese Rokkishu); brought into Kyokushin by Mas Oyama
origin_place: Naha, Okinawa; Kyokushin version Tokyo, Japan
introduced_by: Chojun Miyagi (created); Mas Oyama (brought)
provenance: Oyama prized Tensho above all forms, writing that it was 'the most indispensable of the advanced kata' and the distillation of karate's hard-soft principle; it entered Kyokushin directly from his Goju-ryu training. The kata is Miyagi's composition, so its presence in Kyokushin is transmission, not creation. Kyokushin recension of Miyagi's kata. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan, world-oyama. CANONICAL FORM: 'Tensho' (existing naha-te row, which already lists kyokushin).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensh%C5%8D_(kata) | https://uskyokushin.com/kyokushin-kata | http://the-martial-way.com/history-of-kyokushin-kata/

name: Tsuki no Kata
variants: Kihon Tsuki no kata; Tsuki no kata
meaning: 'Kata of punches' (or 'of thrusts'): a form built almost entirely from stepping punches, symbolising fortune arriving with each decisive strike in Kyokushin lore.
era: mid-20th century (Seigokan founded 1945); in Kyokushin by the 1960s-70s
origin_person: Seigo Tada, founder of Seigokan Goju-ryu
introduced_by: Seigo Tada (created); Tadashi Nakamura (brought)
provenance: Created by Seigo Tada as Kihon Tsuki no kata, one of two Seigokan founder-kata; how it entered Kyokushin is not securely documented, and the common attribution to Tadashi Nakamura as creator is an error, though he is plausibly the conduit given his Goju background (speculative, flagged as such in Kyokushin histories). [Verifier: Creator confirmed: Seigo Tada of Seigokan Goju-ryu (where it is Kihon Punching kata adopted from the Goju-kai line. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan, world-oyama. The seigokan id already on the row is correct and worth keeping: Oyama took Tsuki no Kata from the Goju side, and Seigokan holds its own version.

name: Yantsu
meaning: Usually written with characters read as 'safe three' and glossed in Kyokushin as 'to keep pure', striving to maintain integrity of principle under pressure; the etymology is debated.
origin_person: uncertain; plausibly adapted by Mas Oyama from the kata Ansan/Hansan of Motobu-ha Shito-ryu
introduced_by: Mas Oyama (standardised)
provenance: The most origin-disputed kata in Kyokushin: style histories suggest descent from Ansan (Hansan) preserved in Motobu-ha Shito-ryu, modified by Oyama, but no primary documentation settles the question, so all accounts should be treated as provisional. It appears in no mainstream Okinawan syllabus outside these lines. A Kyokushin signature kata of uncertain origin. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan, world-oyama. A Kyokushin-specific southern kata, universal across the kata-retaining branches.
sources: http://the-martial-way.com/history-of-kyokushin-kata/ | https://kyokushin.fandom.com/wiki/Kata | https://uskyokushin.com/kyokushin-kata

name: Aragaki no Seisan
era: demonstrated 24 March 1867; the earliest dated appearance of Seisan anywhere
origin_person: Unknown Chinese source; brought to Okinawa or composed by Aragaki Seisho (Tsuji Pechin, 1840-1918/1920) of Kume
modifier: Tsuyoshi Chitose (Chito-ryu recension); Ryusho Sakagami and Kenwa Mabuni for the Shito-ryu holdings of Aragaki's kata
provenance: Aragaki demonstrated Seisan (entered in the programme as jusanpo) at the Ochayagoten in the East Garden of Shuri Castle on 24 March 1867, in honour of Zhao Xin, the last Sapposhi. McCarthy translated the programme into English in 1994. This is the only hard 19th-century date in the complex, and the performer is a Kume/Naha man - which is why the Shuri-primacy tradition is on weak ground. Aragaki's kata set (Sochin, Niseishi, Seisan, Unsu) passed to Mabuni, Chitose, Toyama Kanken and others; he taught Higaonna Kanryo for three years from 1867 before referring him to Kojo Taite.

meaning: 'Earth piercing'; one of the Kojo-ryu heaven/earth/void triad with Tenkan and Kukan

origin_person: Not recorded by name. The Kojo family maintained a dojo in Kume and trained at the Ryukyukan in Fuzhou; the family's known Chinese teacher of that generation is Iwah, and the lineage graph already carries an Iwah to Kaho Kojo edge at high confidence
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China, via the Kojo family's Ryukyukan connection; brought to Kume, Naha
modifier: Kaho Kojo, who imported and fitted the kata to the family curriculum; Saikyo Kojo (1873-1941) subsequently introduced material from other Okinawan styles, sumo and sai-jutsu into the family style

provenance: Kojo-ryu is a closed family system of Kume Chinese descent whose distinctive kata are Tenkan, Kukan, Chikan, Hakutsuru, Hakuryu and Hakko. The postures of the Kojo-ryu kata are named for the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac.

name: Gekisai Ni
meaning: attack and smash, two
introduced_by: Chojun Miyagi (created)
provenance: Companion to Gekisai Ichi, adding open-hand and neko-ashi work; Miyagi's own composition.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Gekisai dai ichi
variants: Gekisai (Fukyu) kata I; Geksai dai; Kyokushin: Gekisai dai
meaning: Attack and smash, number one. A deliberately simple popularisation kata: direct blocks, lunging punches and kicks designed to teach schoolchildren and beginners quickly.
introduced_by: Chojun Miyagi (created)
provenance: Created in 1940 for the karate promotion committee convened under Okinawa governor Hayakawa Gen, as Naha-te's contribution to a common beginner syllabus alongside Shoshin Nagamine's Fukyugata ichi. Later absorbed into Kyokushin as Gekisai dai. Miyagi created it in 1940 as a promotional kata for school and beginner instruction. Added ikga, imgka, jundokan-international, okinawa-goju-ryu-kyokai, seigokan, seiwakai, shito-ryu, shito-kai. First of Miyagi Chojun's twelve. The row already listed the dojo-level bodies (Jundokan, Meibukan, Shoreikan, Shodokan) but omitted the international organisational ids that head those same lines.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gekisai | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C5%8Dj%C5%AB-ry%C5%AB

name: Gekisai dai ni
variants: Gekisai (Fukyu) kata II; Kyokushin: Gekisai sho
meaning: Attack and smash, number two. Extends Gekisai dai ichi with open-hand techniques, mawashi-uke and neko-ashi-dachi, introducing the softer receiving methods characteristic of Goju-ryu.
introduced_by: Chojun Miyagi (created)
provenance: Companion kata to Gekisai dai ichi from the same 1940 popularisation programme; the pair are Miyagi's last compositions and the standard entry point of the modern Goju curriculum. Introduces open-hand technique and neko-ashi-dachi to the beginner. Added ikga, imgka, jundokan-international, okinawa-goju-ryu-kyokai, seigokan, seiwakai, shito-ryu, shito-kai. Second of the twelve.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gekisai | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C5%8Dj%C5%AB-ry%C5%AB

name: Genbu
meaning: 'dark warrior' / black tortoise-snake (guardian of the north)
modifier: Meitoku Yagi, with later codification attributed in part to his sons
introduced_by: Meitoku Yagi (created); Meitatsu Yagi (standardised)
provenance: Bishop, Goju-ryu chapter, Meibukan section, and Appendix C
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Meibukan) and Appendix C

era: Chinese origin, undated; brought to Okinawa by Shinko Matayoshi c. 1911-1934
introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted)
provenance: Matayoshi school's 'Kingairyu Tudi-jutsu – kata' table (supplied Guarelli text)

meaning: 'fifty-four'
era: Chinese origin, undated; brought to Okinawa by Shinko Matayoshi c. 1911-1934
introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted)
provenance: Matayoshi school's 'Kingairyu Tudi-jutsu – kata' table (supplied Guarelli text), where it is given as 五十四 Gojushi (Useshi)

name: Hafa
meaning: uncertain; a Fujianese form name preserved in Okinawan pronunciation
origin_person: unknown; Kojo family transmission from Fujian
introduced_by: Kaho Kojo (brought); Kafu Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: One of the supplementary Kojo-ryu kata beyond the six core forms. Kojo Kaho (1849-1925) trained in Fuzhou in the fourth family generation, and the supplementary group is generally attributed to material he imported.
sources: https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html | https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B9%96%E5%9F%8E%E6%B5%81

name: Hakkaku
variants: Hakkaku (white crane); distinct from the Matayoshi/Gokenki Hakkaku-Hakucho crane kata of the same name
meaning: White crane. Third and highest animal kata of Kojo-ryu, expressing evasive footwork and wing-like simultaneous deflection and strike.
era: undocumented; family tradition reaches back to the 18th century
origin_person: Kojo family tradition ascribes the animal kata to the lineage of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China
introduced_by: Kojo UEKATA (brought)
provenance: Completes the tiger-dragon-crane triad; extended Kojo-ryu lists also record Hafa, Nepai, Nunfa, Paichu and other Fujian-named forms, consistent with the family's Kume-village Chinese heritage but thinly documented. Kojo-ryu is grouped here with Naha-te as Kuninda-di for cladogram purposes. [Verifier: Exists; 'white crane', highest animal kata, correct in meaning and character. Same caveat: the Koj
sources: https://www.karatedomagazine.com/2018/12/14/kojo-ryu-karate/ | https://spiritofthekata.com/karate-kata-hakkaku-kojo-ryu/ | https://simonechierchini.com/2020/04/29/kojo-ryu-karate-lo-stile-fantasma-di-okinawa/

name: Hakkaku (Go Kenki den)
meaning: 'white crane'
era: Qing-era Fujian; in Okinawa c. 1912-1940 via Go Kenki; restricted transmission after 1997
modifier: Shinpo Matayoshi (who demonstrated an abridged public version and withheld the full form)
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Shinko Matayoshi (transmitted); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted); Yoshiaki Gakiya (transmitted)
provenance: Matayoshi Kodokan internal record, reported in the supplied Guarelli text; Bishop treats the Gokenki crane material in his Chinese-influence sections but does not name this form.
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix A

name: Hakko
variants: Byakko; Hakko (white tiger); Hakko-ken; Hakuko; Hakukoken
meaning: 'White Tiger'
era: family tradition claims 17th-18th century; documented only in the 20th
origin_person: Kojo family tradition, ascribed to the line of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong, 1656-1737)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China
modified_era: 20th century, when Kojo Kafu (1909-1996) taught outside the family
introduced_by: Kojo UEKATA (brought); Kaho Kojo (transmitted); Kafu Kojo (standardised)
provenance: One of the three animal kata of Kojo-ryu, alongside Hakuryu (White Dragon) and Hakutsuru (White Crane). Kojo-ryu is a Kume village family art descended from the Thirty-Six Families sent from Fujian, and it claims descent from Cai Jia Quan.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B9%96%E5%9F%8E%E6%B5%81 | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html | http://www.budopedia.de/wiki/Koj%C5%8D_ry%C5%AB

name: Hakucho
variants: Haku Cho; Hakuchu; Hakutcho; Paihok; White Swan
meaning: 'White Swan'
era: brought to Okinawa between c. 1912 and 1940
modified_era: 1920s-1930s, as Mabuni absorbed Gokenki's crane material into Shito-ryu
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Kenwa Mabuni (standardised); Tokashiki Iken (transmitted); Kanki Izumigawa (transmitted); Seko Higa (transmitted)
provenance: A Fujian white crane form taught on Okinawa by the Fuzhou tea merchant Gokenki (1886-1940), who worked through the Ryukyu Tode Kenkyukai and taught Mabuni, Miyagi, Kyoda and Matayoshi among others. Mabuni Kenwa took it into Shito-ryu; Tokashiki Iken preserved it in Gohaku-kai.
sources: https://fightingarts.com/interview-with-hohan-soken-the-last-of-the-great-old-time-karate-warriors-part-1/ | https://www.karatebyjesse.com/go-kenki-the-undercover-kung-fu-pioneer-of-okinawan-karate/ | https://karatetim.com/white-crane-of-go-kenki | https://theimss.org/hohansoken/

name: Hakuryu
meaning: 'White Dragon'
era: family tradition; documented in the 20th century
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China
introduced_by: Kojo UEKATA (brought); Kaho Kojo (brought); Kafu Kojo (standardised); Shigeru Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: One of the three animal kata of Kojo-ryu with Hakko (White Tiger) and Hakutsuru (White Crane). Japanese sources describe Hakuryu as containing the dragon, serpent, rat, horse and hare postures.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B9%96%E5%9F%8E%E6%B5%81 | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html | http://www.budopedia.de/wiki/Koj%C5%8D_ry%C5%AB

name: Hakutsuru Heiho Nidan no Koto
meaning: 'the matter of white crane strategy, second level'
era: Qing-era Fujian; in Okinawa c. 1912-1940 via Go Kenki
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Shinko Matayoshi (transmitted); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted)
provenance: Matayoshi school's published Go Kenki kata table (supplied Guarelli text)

provenance: Matayoshi school's published Go Kenki kata table (supplied Guarelli text)

name: Hakutsuru Heiho Shodan no Koto
meaning: 'the matter of white crane strategy, first level'
era: Qing-era Fujian; in Okinawa c. 1912-1940 via Go Kenki
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Shinko Matayoshi (transmitted); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted)
provenance: Matayoshi school's published Go Kenki kata table (supplied Guarelli text); Bishop discusses the Gokenki white crane material but does not tabulate these titles.
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix A and the Matsumura Seito chapter (for the competing Hakutsuru claim)

name: Han
meaning: the USA Goju reading of Anan
introduced_by: Peter Urban (created)
provenance: USA Goju-ryu. Practised as that school's version of the Ryuei-ryu kata Anan.
sources: https://www.karatebyjesse.com/ryuei-ryu-history-ramblings-kata-anan/

name: Happoren
variants: Babulian; Hakkoren; Paipuren; Paipuren (Shito-ryu); Pappuren; Papuren
meaning: 'eight consecutive/linked steps'
era: Qing-era Fujian; brought to Okinawa c. 1912 when Go Kenki settled in Naha; taught there until his death in 1940
origin_person: Go Kenki (Wu Xianhui), Fujian white crane boxer resident in Naha
modifier: Kenwa Mabuni (Shito-ryu adaptation, as Paipuren); Shinko and Shinpo Matayoshi (Matayoshi-line retention)
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Kenwa Mabuni (modified); Shinko Matayoshi (transmitted); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted); Kenwa Mabuni (standardised); Tokashiki Iken (transmitted)

sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix A (Chinese boxing forms) and the Gokenki material in the Goju-ryu / To'on-ryu chapters

name: Haufa
meaning: uncertain; commonly rendered 'supreme wind'
era: early to mid 20th century in Okinawa
origin_person: Disputed; associated with the Fujian white-crane material transmitted by Gokenki (Wu Xiangui) and preserved in the Izumigawa/Senbukan and Motobu-ha Shito-ryu lines
modifier: Shogo Kuniba / Motobu-ha Shito-ryu competition form
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Kanki Izumigawa (transmitted); Shogo Kuniba (standardised)
provenance: Chinese white-crane import; fixed for tournament use in Japanese Shito-ryu organisations.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Heiku
meaning: white tiger
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko of Fuzhou; ultimate creator unknown
modifier: Kenko Nakaima, who ended the family-secret transmission in 1971; Tsuguo Sakumoto, who fixed the competition form
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised); Tsuguo Sakumoto (standardised); Teruo Hayashi (brought)
provenance: Ryuei-ryu: Nakaima Norisato studied in Fuzhou in the 1840s
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

meaning: 'urgent response form one' (also glossed as a Shoreikan basic form)
introduced_by: Seikichi Toguchi (created)
provenance: Bishop, Goju-ryu chapter, Shoreikan section, and Appendix C, where the Shoreikan column carries a set of kata found in no other Goju branch.
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Shoreikan) and Appendix C | Toguchi, Okinawan Goju-ryu (1976)

name: Hookiyu Kata Ni
meaning: 'urgent response form two'
introduced_by: Seikichi Toguchi (created)
provenance: Bishop, Goju-ryu chapter, Shoreikan section, and Appendix C
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Shoreikan) and Appendix C | Toguchi, Okinawan Goju-ryu (1976)

name: Ippyakureihachi (Kojo-ryu)
meaning: 'One hundred and eight'
era: family transmission; discussed in modern Okinawan scholarship
introduced_by: Kaho Kojo (brought); Kafu Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: The Kojo family version of the 108 form, cognate with Goju-ryu's Suparinpei and To'on-ryu's Pechurin. Its existence is the main evidence that the Kojo line drew on the same Fujian 108 tradition as the Higaonna line rather than an entirely separate one.
sources: https://medium.com/@motobu715/ippyakureihachi-of-koj%C5%8D-ry%C5%AB-dd0a9ca50010 | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html

name: Jin-i
meaning: 'man position'
era: Undocumented; Kojo family tradition claims 17th-18th century Kume origins

introduced_by: Kojo UEKATA (brought); Kaho Kojo (transmitted); Kafu Kojo (standardised)
provenance: Bishop, Kojo-ryu chapter and Appendix C
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Kojo-ryu chapter and Appendix C

name: Jion (To'on-ryu)
meaning: Traditionally read as the name of a temple or of the monk Jion
era: learned by Kyoda in the early 20th century; in the To'on-ryu syllabus from 1934
introduced_by: Kentsu Yabu (transmitted); Juhatsu Kyoda (brought)
provenance: The one Shuri-te form in an otherwise wholly Naha-te syllabus. Kyoda Juhatsu learned it from Yabu Kentsu (1866-1937), not from Higaonna, and carried it into To'on-ryu.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Don-ry%C5%AB | https://isshin-concentration.blogspot.com/2023/08/toon-ryu.html | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html

introduced_by: Seikichi Toguchi (created)

sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Shoreikan) and Appendix C | Toguchi, Okinawan Goju-ryu (1976)

name: Kakuha Dai Ni
meaning: 'break through at a distance, second'
introduced_by: Seikichi Toguchi (created)
provenance: Bishop, Goju-ryu chapter, Shoreikan section, and Appendix C
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Shoreikan) and Appendix C

name: Kakuho
meaning: 'Crane method'
modified_era: late 20th century, as Gohaku-kai was formed in 1982
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Tokashiki Iken (transmitted)
provenance: One of the crane forms in the Gokenki group preserved on Okinawa, alongside Hakucho, Haffa, Hakkaku, Hakutsuru and Happoren. Tokashiki Iken (b. 1938) has been the principal modern researcher of this material and also produced one of the important Japanese editions of the Bubishi.
sources: https://www.karatebyjesse.com/go-kenki-the-undercover-kung-fu-pioneer-of-okinawan-karate/ | https://karatetim.com/white-crane-of-go-kenki | https://springthundertaiji.com/hakutsuru-okinawan-white-crane

name: Kan'yu Seisan
era: 19th century Naha; transmitted into To'on-ryu from 1934
provenance: Kyoda Juhatsu knew two Seisans - Higaonna Kanryo's (the Goju ancestor) and Higaonna Kan'yu's, Kanryo's older relative and possibly Kyoda's first teacher through his mother's family. He vacillated over which to transmit, at one point proposing to combine the best of both, and ultimately taught Kanzaki Shigekazu only the Kan'yu version. To'on-ryu's own syllabus lists it as 'Kan'yu Seisan'. Kanryo's version is lost from this line.

name: Kiso Ichi and Ni
variants: Kiso I; Kiso II; Kiso Kata
meaning: 'Foundation one and two'
introduced_by: Juhatsu Kyoda (created)
provenance: Paired introductory forms in To'on-ryu, functionally parallel to Miyagi's Gekisai pair in Goju-ryu and to Kanei Uechi's bridging kata: postwar teaching aids built to make a Chinese-derived syllabus teachable to beginners.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Don-ry%C5%AB | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html

introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted)
provenance: Matayoshi school's 'Kingairyu Tudi-jutsu – kata' table (supplied Guarelli text)

name: Kotsuru
meaning: 'tiger and crane'
era: Chinese origin, undated; brought to Okinawa by Shinko Matayoshi c. 1911-1934
introduced_by: Shinko Matayoshi (brought); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted)

variants: Ku no Maki; Ku no kata (void/sky form); Kumaki
meaning: 'Void piercing' / 'sky piercing'; second of the Kojo-ryu triad
era: imported into the Kojo family style in the fourth generation, i.e. within the lifetime of Kaho Kojo (1849-1925)
origin_person: Not recorded by name; same Fuzhou provenance as Chikan and Tenkan, with Iwah the family's documented Chinese teacher of that generation
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China; brought to Kume, Naha
modifier: Kaho Kojo; later family reworking under Saikyo Kojo and Kafu Kojo
modified_era: import c. 1870s-1900; family reworking early-to-mid 20th century
introduced_by: Iwah (transmitted); Kaho Kojo (brought); Kafu Kojo (transmitted); Kojo UEKATA (brought); Kafu Kojo (standardised); Shigeru Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: See Chikan. Kukan is normally taught as the middle member of the Tenkan/Kukan/Chikan set, the three kata specifically recorded as fourth-generation imports rather than ancestral family material.
sources: https://www.karatedomagazine.com/2018/12/14/kojo-ryu-karate/ | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Kururunfa
meaning: Uncertain; commonly glossed 'holding on long and striking suddenly' or 'forever stopping and tearing'. The name is a phonetic Okinawan rendering of Chinese and the glosses are later
origin_person: Unknown Chinese originator; transmitted to Kanryo Higaonna in Fuzhou by Ryu Ryu Ko
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised)
provenance: One of the Higaonna-lineage kaishu kata, notable for its open-hand and muchimi close-range work. Like Saifa, it is absent from To'on-ryu, which weakens the claim that it came directly from Higaonna and raises the same authorship question.
sources: https://togkfnz.org/about-togkf/goju-ryu-kata/ | https://www.houstonkarate.org/benefits/kata-of-goju-ryu | https://www.jissenkarate.com/goju-ryu-kata/ | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Nepai
variants: Neipai; Nepai (Ryuei-ryu — separate transmission); Nijuhachi; Nipai; Nipaipo; Nipaipo (二十八歩, Mabuni's Shito-ryu adaptation)
meaning: 'twenty-eight'
era: Qing-era Fujian; brought to Okinawa by Go Kenki, taught in Naha c. 1912-1940
modifier: Kenwa Mabuni (renamed Nipaipo and adapted for Shito-ryu); Juhatsu Kyoda (To'on-ryu form); Shinko and Shinpo Matayoshi (Go Kenki-line form)
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Juhatsu Kyoda (standardised); Kenwa Mabuni (renamed); Shinko Matayoshi (transmitted)
provenance: Existing database entry, confirmed and extended from the Matayoshi Go Kenki kata table in the supplied Guarelli text
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, To'on-ryu chapter and Appendix C

name: Nijikken
meaning: uncertain
introduced_by: Kaho Kojo (brought); Shuren Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: Supplementary Kojo-ryu kata, transmitted within the family line running Kojo Isei (1832-1891), Taitei (1837-1917), Kaho (1849-1925), Saikyo (1873-1941), Shuren (1883-1945) and Kafu (1909-1996).
sources: https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html

name: Niseishi (Ryuei-ryu)
variants: Niseshi; cognate with Aragaki Niseishi / Nijushiho but a distinct transmission
meaning: Twenty-four (steps/hands). The Ryuei-ryu version of a Fuzhou form also transmitted separately by Aragaki Seisho (whence Shito-ryu's Niseishi and Shotokan's Nijushiho).
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
introduced_by: Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised)
provenance: Listed in the Ryuei-ryu (Ryuho-kai) curriculum alongside Sanchin, Seisan and Sanseiru; its coexistence with Seisho Arakaki's independent Niseishi line supports a shared Fuzhou source pool rather than a single Okinawan origin. Added ryuei-ryu-hozonkai and ryuei-ryu-ryuhokai, for consistency with the other Ryuei-ryu rows (Anan, Anan Dai, Ohan, Ohan Dai, Paiho all carry the Hozonkai id). CANONICAL FORM: 'Niseishi'.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ry%C5%ABei-ry%C5%AB | https://onlinemartialarts.org/okinawa-ryuei-ryu-karate-kobudo-ryuho-kai-kata/ | http://www.budopedia.de/wiki/Ry%C5%ABei_ry%C5%AB

name: Paiku
meaning: white crane
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko of Fuzhou; ultimate creator unknown
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised); Tsuguo Sakumoto (standardised); Teruo Hayashi (brought)
provenance: Ryuei-ryu family transmission, made public by the third generation.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Pechurin
variants: Ippyaku Reihachi; Pecchurin; Peichurin; Suparinpei (To'on-ryu); Bechurin; Petchurin
meaning: Okinawan reading of 108; the Goju-ryu name for the same lineage form is Suparinpei
era: transmitted from Higaonna Kanryo between 1902 and 1915
modified_era: 1934-1968, as the To'on-ryu syllabus was fixed
introduced_by: Kanryo Higaonna (transmitted); Juhatsu Kyoda (brought)
provenance: To'on-ryu's senior kata. Kyoda Juhatsu entered Higaonna Kanryo's dojo in 1902 and stayed until Higaonna's death in 1915, longer than Miyagi Chojun; he preserved the form under the older Okinawan name Pechurin rather than Miyagi's Suparinpei. Kyoda founded To'on-ryu in 1934, naming it after Higaonna.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Don-ry%C5%AB | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html | https://translesbian.wordpress.com/2013/05/30/kyoda-juhatsu-and-the-evolution-of-toon-goju-ryu/

name: Pechurin Dai
provenance: NONE. No federation, no syllabus, no publication.

name: Peichurin
meaning: 'hundred linked steps' / '108'
era: Qing-era Fujian; taught in Naha from c. 1880s-1900s; preserved in To'on-ryu from c. 1902 onwards
origin_person: Unknown Fujian original; transmitted to Okinawa through Ryu Ryu Ko's teaching of Higaonna Kanryo
modifier: Juhatsu Kyoda (preserved the Higaonna form without Miyagi's later revisions)
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Juhatsu Kyoda (standardised)
provenance: Bishop, To'on-ryu chapter and Appendix C: Bishop lists the To'on-ryu syllabus as Sanchin, Sesan, Sanseiru, Jion, Nepai and Peichurin.
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, To'on-ryu chapter and Appendix C

name: Rokkishu
meaning: 'Six machine hands' or 'six subtle hands'
era: early 20th century transmission; in To'on-ryu from 1934
origin_person: unknown; Fujian open-hand tradition, possibly via Gokenki
introduced_by: Juhatsu Kyoda (brought); Gokenki (transmitted)
provenance: Open-hand rotating exercise preserved in To'on-ryu. The same material underlies the six-hand sequences that Miyagi Chojun built into Tensho, which makes it evidence for the shared Naha environment of the 1910s-1920s rather than for a single inventor.
sources: https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Don-ry%C5%AB

name: Saifa
meaning: smash and tear
era: Qing-era China; in Naha from the 1880s
origin_person: Unknown Fujian originator; transmitted through Ryu Ryu Ko to Kanryo Higaonna
modified_era: c. 1920s-1930s, when Miyagi fixed the Goju kaishugata syllabus
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Chojun Miyagi (created)
provenance: Fuzhou to Naha via Higaonna; formalised as one of Miyagi's eight kaishugata.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Sanchin
variants: Saam Chien; Sam Chien (Fujian saam chin); Sanchin (Goju); Sanchin (Goju-ryu, closed fist); Sanchin (Kyokushin); Sanchin (Ryuei-ryu); Sanchin (To'on-ryu); Sanchin (Uechi); Sanchin (Uechi-ryu, open hand); Sanchin dai ichi / dai ni (Goju); Uechi Sanchin
meaning: 'Three battles' or 'three conflicts', variously read as mind/body/spirit or as three points of contact
era: Qing-era China; taught in Naha from c. 1880s
origin_person: Unknown Chinese originator. Transmitted to Kanryo Higaonna in Fuzhou by the teacher known on Okinawa as Ryu Ryu Ko, and independently to Kanbun Uechi by Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe)
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China; Southern Chinese hard-qigong and Crane/Tiger boxing traditions
modifier: Chojun Miyagi, who converted the open-hand nukite to closed fists, removed the turns, and slowed the breathing to produce the Goju-ryu form. Juhatsu Kyoda is credited by some accounts with making the closed-fist change first
modified_era: Miyagi's revision c. 1910s-1930s; Uechi-ryu retains the original open-hand form
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe) (transmitted); Kanbun Uechi (brought); Juhatsu Kyoda (modified); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Chojun Miyagi (modified)
provenance: Higaonna returned from Fuzhou c. 1881 with Sanchin as the foundation kata of Naha-te; Kanbun Uechi returned from Fujian c. 1910 with a separate open-hand Sanchin from the Pangai-noon line. Both descend from the same Fujian family of hard-qigong forms but are not the same kata. The Goju-ryu closed-fist Sanchin is a 20th-century Okinawan revision, not the imported form.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanryo_Higaonna | https://tokkarateri.webs.com/historyofsanchin.htm | https://ymaa.com/articles/sanchin-kata-ancient-wisdom | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shisochin

name: Sanchin (Ryuei-ryu)
meaning: 'Three battles'
modified_era: 1971, when the family syllabus was codified for public teaching
introduced_by: Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenchu Nakaima (transmitted); Kenko Nakaima (standardised)
provenance: The Ryuei-ryu foundation kata, a third independent Okinawan line of Sanchin alongside the Higaonna/Miyagi and Uechi transmissions. Performed with open hands and a distinct turning pattern, and taught inside the Nakaima house for three generations before 1971.
sources: https://www.karatebyjesse.com/ryuei-ryu-history-ramblings-kata-anan/ | https://fullpotentialma.com/ryuei-ryu-okinawan-karate/ | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryuei-ry%C5%AB

name: Sanchin (To'on-ryu)
meaning: 'three battles' / 'three conflicts'
era: Qing-era Fujian; Naha from c. 1880s; fixed as the To'on-ryu form from c. 1902-1930s
origin_person: Unknown Fujian original transmitted by Ryu Ryu Ko to Higaonna Kanryo
modifier: Juhatsu Kyoda (retained Higaonna's open-hand, turning version)
introduced_by: Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Juhatsu Kyoda (standardised)
provenance: Bishop, To'on-ryu chapter; the To'on-ryu Sanchin is tabulated separately in Appendix C because it differs materially from the Goju-ryu form.
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, To'on-ryu and Goju-ryu chapters, Appendix C

name: Sanseiru
variants: Sandairui; Sanseiryu (distinct, Uechi); Sanseirū; Sanseru; Sanseryu
meaning: thirty-six hands
era: Qing-era China; in Naha from c. 1880s
origin_person: Unknown Fujian originator; transmitted through Ryu Ryu Ko
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Norisato Nakaima (brought)
provenance: Two independent Okinawan imports of the same Fuzhou material: the Higaonna line (Goju) and the Nakaima line (Ryuei-ryu).
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Seienchin
meaning: to control and pull into battle
era: Qing-era China; in Naha from the 1880s
origin_person: Unknown Fujian originator; transmitted through Ryu Ryu Ko to Kanryo Higaonna
modifier: Chojun Miyagi (Goju line); Kenwa Mabuni (Shito line)
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Kenwa Mabuni (transmitted)
provenance: Higaonna line; passed into Shito-ryu through Mabuni's study under Higaonna, which is why WKF lists it for both Goju and Shito.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Seipai
meaning: eighteen hands
era: Qing-era China; in Naha from the 1880s
origin_person: Unknown Fujian originator; transmitted through Ryu Ryu Ko to Kanryo Higaonna
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised)
provenance: Higaonna line, fixed by Miyagi in the Goju kaishugata set.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Seiryu (Meibukan)
meaning: 'blue/green dragon' (guardian of the east)
modifier: Meitoku Yagi, with later codification attributed in part to his sons
introduced_by: Meitoku Yagi (created); Meitatsu Yagi (standardised)
provenance: Bishop, Goju-ryu chapter, Meibukan section, and Appendix C
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Meibukan) and Uechi-ryu chapter, Appendix C

name: Seisan (Ryuei-ryu)
meaning: 'Thirteen'
introduced_by: Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised); Tsuguo Sakumoto (transmitted)
provenance: Second of the Ryuei-ryu foundation pair with Sanchin, preceding the six signature forms (Heiku, Paiku, Pachu, Ohan, Paiho, Anan). Distinct from both the Shuri-te and the Goju-ryu Seisan.
sources: https://fullpotentialma.com/ryuei-ryu-okinawan-karate/ | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryuei-ry%C5%AB

name: Seiyunchin
meaning: Variously 'to control and pull into battle', 'to suppress and pull'; the reading is contested
origin_person: Unknown. Chinese antecedent assumed, transmitted through Kanryo Higaonna's Fuzhou training with Ryu Ryu Ko
modifier: Chojun Miyagi, who fixed the Goju-ryu form
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Kenwa Mabuni (transmitted)
provenance: One of the Higaonna-lineage kaishu kata, distinctive for containing no kicks and for its heavy shiko-dachi work. Preserved in Goju-ryu and, in a different shape, in Shito-ryu via Mabuni's study under both Higaonna and Miyagi.
sources: https://togkfnz.org/about-togkf/goju-ryu-kata/ | https://www.houstonkarate.org/benefits/kata-of-goju-ryu | https://www.karatephilosophy.com/a-complete-list-of-goju-ryu-karate-katas-with-videos/ | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Sepai
meaning: 'Eighteen' (eighteen hands); part of the Fujian numerical kata family with Sanseiru, Seisan and Suparinpei
origin_person: Unknown Chinese originator; transmitted to Kanryo Higaonna in Fuzhou by Ryu Ryu Ko
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised)
provenance: Sepai belongs to the numerically named Fujian set (13, 18, 36, 108) that is the clearest structural evidence of the Chinese origin of Naha-te. The number is usually read as 6 x 3, the six directions by the three levels, rather than a literal count of techniques.
sources: https://togkfnz.org/about-togkf/goju-ryu-kata/ | https://www.jissenkarate.com/goju-ryu-kata/ | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Sesan
variants: Hangetsu and Shuri Seisan are cognate but distinct Shuri/Tomari forms; Seisan (Naha lineage); Sēsan; Seisan (Goju-ryu); Naha Seisan
meaning: Thirteen (hands), variously explained as thirteen techniques or 13 as an auspicious number. The Naha version emphasises close-range hard-soft striking, low kicks and heavy rooted stepping.
modifier: Kanryo Higaonna; Chojun Miyagi, who fixed its late position in the post-war Goju sequence
introduced_by: Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Juhatsu Kyoda (standardised); Norisato Nakaima (brought)
provenance: CORRECTION, TWO FAULTS. (1) FIELD ERROR: the present row has the era string 'Qing-era China; Okinawa from c. 1880s' sitting in the `modifier` column and no modifier recorded. Moved to era; Higaonna and Miyagi entered as modifiers. (2) toon-ryu removed from the style list: To'on-ryu practises Higaonna Kan'yu's Seisan, a different form, now entered as 'Kan'yu Seisan'. ryuei-ryu also removed - Ryuei-ryu has its own row and its relation to this one is disputed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seisan | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Don-ry%C5%AB | https://fightingarts.com/unraveling-the-mysteries-of-the-nafadi-tradition-its-kata/

name: Shiho Uke
meaning: 'Four-direction receiving'; also listed as Tsuki-uke
introduced_by: Juhatsu Kyoda (created)
provenance: Four-direction blocking form in the To'on-ryu curriculum, listed alongside Ten-i Happo and the Kiso pair as the preparatory group before Sanchin.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Don-ry%C5%AB | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html

name: Shisochin
meaning: 'Fighting in four directions' / 'four-way battle'
origin_person: Unknown. Standardly credited to Ryu Ryu Ko's teaching of Kanryo Higaonna, but a competing account holds that a version was already circulating on Okinawa through Seisho Aragaki
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China, or Naha via the Aragaki line
modifier: Chojun Miyagi, for whom Shisochin was reportedly a favourite kata in later life
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Seisho Arakaki (Aragaki) (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised)
provenance: The Higaonna/Ryu Ryu Ko route is the Goju-ryu house account. The Aragaki route is supported by the presence of related material in lines descending from Seisho Aragaki (1840-1918), who taught a Chinese-derived repertoire independently of Higaonna and who demonstrated before the last Sapposhi in 1867.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shisochin | https://togkfnz.org/about-togkf/goju-ryu-kata/ | https://www.gkrkarate.com/about-gkr/brown-belt-1st-kyu/introduction-to-kata-sanseru/

name: Shujaku
meaning: 'vermilion bird' (guardian of the south)
modifier: Meitoku Yagi, with later codification attributed in part to his sons
introduced_by: Meitoku Yagi (created); Meitatsu Yagi (standardised)
provenance: Bishop, Goju-ryu chapter, Meibukan section, and Appendix C
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Meibukan) and Appendix C

name: Suparinpei
native: 壱百零八 / スーパーリンペイ
variants: Bechurin; Hyaku Hachi Ho; Hyakuhachiho; Pecchurin (To'on-ryu); Pechurin; Pechurin (ペッチュウリン, To'on-ryu); Suparimpei; Suparinpei (Goju-ryu); Sūpārinpei; Pecchurin; Peichurin; Bechurin (ベッチューリン); Sūpārinpai; Ippyakureihachi (Japanese reading, pre-1934)
renamed_from: Pechurin / Peichurin (一百零八 / 百歩連)
meaning: 'One hundred and eight'; in the Fujian tradition linked to the 108 vital points and to the 108 stars of Chinese cosmology
era: Qing-era China; taught in Naha from c. 1880s
origin_person: Unknown Chinese originator; transmitted to Kanryo Higaonna in Fuzhou by Ryu Ryu Ko
modifier: Chojun Miyagi, who fixed the Goju-ryu version as the style's culminating kata; Juhatsu Kyoda preserved a parallel version under the older name Pecchurin in To'on-ryu
modified_era: Miyagi's version fixed 1920s-1940s; Kyoda's Pecchurin retains the earlier Higaonna shape
introduced_by: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted); Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Juhatsu Kyoda (transmitted); Juhatsu Kyoda (standardised)
provenance: Suparinpei is the longest kata in the Goju-ryu syllabus and is treated as the parent form from which shorter Naha-te kata were extracted. The To'on-ryu Pecchurin and the Goju-ryu Suparinpei are the two surviving branches of Higaonna's teaching and differ materially, which is the best available evidence for how much Miyagi changed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanryo_Higaonna | https://togkfnz.org/about-togkf/goju-ryu-kata/ | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Tanchin
meaning: uncertain; probably 'single battle', paired conceptually with Sanchin
origin_person: unknown; Kojo family transmission from Fujian
introduced_by: Kaho Kojo (brought); Kafu Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: Supplementary Kojo-ryu kata. The Kojo line's Kume village position gave it direct and repeated Fujian contact into the late 19th century, which is the usual explanation for the number of otherwise unattested Chinese form names in its syllabus.
sources: https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html

name: Ten-i
variants: Tenchijin (the triad taught as one sequence)
meaning: 'heaven position'
era: Undocumented. Kojo family tradition claims descent from the Kume lineage of Kojo Uekata (17th-18th century); no external documentation before the 20th century
origin_person: Kojo family of Kume (Kuninda), Naha; no individual creator named
modifier: Kaho Kojo and Kafu Kojo (form in which it was taught in the 20th century)
introduced_by: Kojo UEKATA (brought); Kaho Kojo (transmitted); Kafu Kojo (standardised); Shigeru Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: Bishop, Kojo-ryu chapter and Appendix C. Bishop is effectively the only English-language source for the Kojo-ryu syllabus, which is why these kata are absent from WKF-derived lists.
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Kojo-ryu chapter and Appendix C

name: Ten-i Happo
meaning: 'Eight directions of shifting position'
introduced_by: Juhatsu Kyoda (created); Kanryo Higaonna (transmitted)
provenance: A short eight-direction movement exercise standing at the head of the To'on-ryu syllabus. Derived from Higaonna's preparatory drills but organised into a named form by Kyoda.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Don-ry%C5%AB | https://isshin-concentration.blogspot.com/2023/08/toon-ryu.html

name: Tenchi
meaning: 'heaven and earth'
era: Second half of the 20th century (Meibukan, after 1963)
introduced_by: Meitoku Yagi (created)
provenance: Bishop, Goju-ryu chapter, Meibukan section, and Appendix C
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Goju-ryu chapter (Meibukan) and Appendix C

name: Tenkan
variants: Ten no Maki; Ten no kata (heaven form); Tenmaki
meaning: 'Heaven piercing'; first of the Kojo-ryu triad
era: imported into the Kojo family style in the fourth generation, i.e. within the lifetime of Kaho Kojo (1849-1925)
origin_person: Not recorded by name; same Fuzhou provenance as Chikan and Kukan, with Iwah the family's documented Chinese teacher of that generation
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China; brought to Kume, Naha
modifier: Kaho Kojo; later family reworking under Saikyo Kojo and Kafu Kojo
modified_era: import c. 1870s-1900; family reworking early-to-mid 20th century
introduced_by: Iwah (transmitted); Kaho Kojo (brought); Kafu Kojo (transmitted); Kojo UEKATA (brought); Kafu Kojo (standardised); Shigeru Kojo (transmitted)
provenance: See Chikan. Tenkan is the best-known of the three and the kata most often shown publicly by Kojo-ryu representatives.
sources: https://www.karatedomagazine.com/2018/12/14/kojo-ryu-karate/ | https://yushikan.blogspot.com/2011/03/koden-and-shinden-kata-of-naha-te.html | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Tensho
meaning: rotating palms
introduced_by: Chojun Miyagi (created)
provenance: Composed by Miyagi from the Rokkishu (six-hands) sequences of the Bubishi, as a soft counterpart to Sanchin.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Tsuruho
meaning: 'crane method'
era: Qing-era Fujian; in Okinawa c. 1912-1940 via Go Kenki
introduced_by: Gokenki (brought); Shinko Matayoshi (transmitted); Shinpo Matayoshi (transmitted)
provenance: Matayoshi school's own published list of the Go Kenki transmission (Shorinha Tsuruken), reproduced in the supplied Guarelli text; consistent with Bishop's account of Gokenki's teaching.
sources: Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix A

name: Urban Kururunfa
introduced_by: Peter Urban (created)
provenance: Urban's reading of Kururunfa for USA Goju-ryu.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Urban_(karate)

name: Urban Taikyoku
introduced_by: Peter Urban (created)
provenance: Urban's reworking of Taikyoku for USA Goju-ryu.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Urban_(karate)

name: Chibana Kūsankū
provenance: tsv. A distinct Kūsankū recension handed from Chibana Chōshō to Tōyama Kanken in 1914, described by Motobu Naoki as an unusual kata of Tōyama's. Worth adding as a named variant alongside Chatan Yara no Kusanku, Kusanku Sho and Tomari Kusanku.

name: Chinen Bo Kihon Ichi
provenance: federation official syllabus + branch syllabus

name: Chinen Bo Kihon Ni
provenance: federation official syllabus

name: Chinen Sai Kihon Ichi
provenance: federation official syllabus

name: Chinen Tonkuwa Kihon Ichi
provenance: federation official syllabus

name: Chishaukin
provenance: Performed by Aragaki Tsuji Pēchin (Aragaki Seishō) at the 1867 Sanrukuchu demonstration and recorded by Mabuni Kenwa as part of Aragaki's curriculum alongside Seisan, Sochin, Unshu and Niseishi. Also rendered Chishaukiun or Chisaukin. One of the very few kata names attested in a dated 19th-century document.

name: Gusukuma no Chinto
era: 19th-century Okinawa; preserved in Gensei-ryu from c. 1950
origin_person: Tomari-te Chinto tradition, transmitted through Gusukuma (Shiroma) of Tomari
provenance: Listed in the Gensei-ryu kata canon as 城間（グスクマ）のチントウ.

name: Kanyū no Seisan
era: transmitted to Kyoda in the early 20th century; one of the six kata Tōon-ryū carries
modifier: Kyoda Jūhatsu, who preserved it unaltered
provenance: Higaonna Kanyū of Higashi-mura, Naha, a relative of the Kyoda family by repeated intermarriage; distinct from the Seisan of Higaonna Kanryō, which Kyoda knew but chose not to transmit in order to avoid duplicating the Gōjū-ryū and Shitō-ryū forms

name: Shukumine no Bassai
era: Passai lineage by the mid-19th century; Shukumine's recension from c. 1950
provenance: Listed in the Gensei-ryu kata canon on the Japanese Wikipedia article as 祝嶺（シュクミネ）の抜塞, with a companion 祝嶺の抜塞小 (Shukumine no Bassai Sho).

name: Ananku
variants: Anaku; Ananko; Anankū; Annanko; Annanku; Ānankū
meaning: peace from the south
era: c. 1930s (some accounts say as early as 1895)
modifier: Chotoku Kyan; the Shorin and Isshin recensions diverge slightly
introduced_by: Chotoku Kyan (created); Shoshin Nagamine (transmitted); Tatsuo Shimabuku (transmitted)
provenance: Traditionally said to derive from material Kyan encountered in Taiwan, hence the 'southern' name.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Annanko
meaning: peace from the south (Shito reading)
origin_person: Chotoku Kyan for the source kata; the Shito-ryu recension via the Kyan line
modifier: Shito-ryu practitioners who fixed the competition version
introduced_by: Chotoku Kyan (created); Kenwa Mabuni (standardised)
provenance: Shito-ryu naming of the Kyan Ananku.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List [row membership uncertain]

name: Channan
variants: Chan Nan; Chiang Nan; Shiraguma/Shiro Kuma identification (per Iwai Tsukuo)
meaning: Meaning unknown; suggested to be a Chinese personal or place name (sometimes rendered Chiang Nan). Significant as the proto-Pinan: the working name or source form from which Itosu built the Pinan series.
origin_person: Anko Itosu (as recorded; possibly reworking older Chinese material)
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created)
provenance: Known chiefly from Motobu Chōki's testimony that Itosu first called his new school kata Channan before settling on Pinan; the original form is lost, and later 'Channan' reconstructions are modern. Iwai Tsukuo (a student of Motobu Chōsei) claimed in 1997 that Motobu's Shiraguma kata preserved the old Channan; this is unverified and should be treated as folklore.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channan | https://www.inkks.org/articles/the-mystery-of-the-channan-kata | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinan

name: Chatan Yara no Kusanku
variants: Chatan Yara Kushanku; Chatanyara Kusanku; Yara Kusanku
meaning: 'Kusanku of Yara of Chatan village': the longest Kusanku version, attributed to Chatan Yara, said to have studied in China; prized for its wide, flowing movement and now a celebrated tournament kata.
introduced_by: Chatan Yara (created); Chotoku Kyan (standardised)
provenance: The attribution to Chatan Yara (1668-1756) is traditional and partly folkloric; the version reached the modern era through Chōtoku Kyan's line (Kyan reportedly learned it from Yara of Chatan's descendants) and so entered Seibukan, Shobayashi, Shōrinji-ryū and Isshin-ryū, and Shitō-ryū via Hayashi-ha. It became world famous through WKF competition. Same form as Chatanyara Kushanku.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%ABsank%C5%AB_(kata) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatan_Yara | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C5%8Dtoku_Kyan

name: Chatanyara Kushanku
variants: Chatan Yara no Kusanku; Kitanya Kushanku
meaning: Chatan Yara's Kusanku
modifier: Chotoku Kyan, and later Shito-ryu competitors who fixed the tournament form
modified_era: early 20th century; competition form from the 1970s
introduced_by: Chatan Yara (created); Chotoku Kyan (transmitted)
provenance: Attributed to Chatan Yara, said to have studied in Fuzhou; carried into Shorin and Shito lines.

name: Chinte

name: Kusanku
native: 公相君 / クーサンクー
variants: Kanku Dai (観空大); Kong Sang Koon (공상군); Koshokun; Kosokun; Kusanku Dai; Kushanku; Kūsankū
meaning: Named after Kūsankū (Kwang Shang Fu), a Chinese envoy/military attaché who visited Okinawa around 1756. Funakoshi's renaming Kankū (観空) means 'to view the sky', after the opening gesture; the kata is regarded as the pinnacle of the Shuri-te repertoire and the ancestor of the Pinan series.
origin_person: Kanga Sakukawa (attributed), after the envoy Kūsankū
introduced_by: Kusanku (brought); Kanga Sakukawa (created); Anko Itosu (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: Tradition (partly folklore, anchored by the 1762 Ōshima Hikki record of a Chinese called Kūsankū demonstrating grappling in Okinawa) holds that Sakugawa composed the kata after studying with the envoy; it passed through Matsumura and Itosu, who standardised the Dai version. Funakoshi renamed it Kankū Dai in the mid-1930s (Karate-dō Kyōhan, 1935); the Korean Kong Sang Koon of Tang Soo Do preserves the Okinawan name. Add chito-ryu. 公相君 appears in the Chito-ryu kata canon given by the Japanese Wikipedia article on the style, sourced to the Chito-ryu sohonbu. Placement varies more than any other Shuri kata: Isshin-ryu teaches it at 3rd kyu and Shotokan examines its recension, Kanku Dai, at 2nd dan. Added shogen-ryu, shorin-ryu-kishaba-juku, ueshiro-shorin-ryu, shorinji-ryu, shito-kai. Eighteenth and most senior of the Matsubayashi 18. Canonical row for 'Kushanku (Wado-ryu)' and for the Shoto

provenance: Itosu reworked the old Kusanku into Dai and Shō versions for systematic teaching; Funakoshi renamed the pair Kankū Dai and Kankū Shō in the mid-1930s. Practised today mainly in Kobayashi Shōrin-ryū, Shitō-ryū and Shotokan. Itosu's shorter companion to the full Kusanku.

name: Matsumura Seisan
variants: Matsumura no Seisan; Seisan (Shito-ryu, Shuri version)

origin_person: Attributed to Sokon Matsumura (1809-1898) by tradition; the attribution is unevidenced
modifier: Ryusho Sakagami, who added it to the Itosu-kai list after learning it from Tsuchiya of the Shudokan; Hohan Soken for the Matsumura Seito line via Nabe Matsumura
provenance: NEW RECORD. Essential because 'the Shito-ryu Seisan' is not one object: Shito-ryu holds this AND the Naha 'Sesan', acquired separately about seventy years apart. Seisan was NOT in Mabuni's original Shuri curriculum - 'In the original curriculum of Shito-ryu this kata did not exist' - and entered post-war when Sakagami Ryusho traced it to the Shudokan (Toyama Kanken's school), learned it from Tsuchiya there, and put it on the Itosu-kai list, from which other Shito-ryu schools took it. The separate Matsumura Seito holding descends via Nabe Matsumura (1860-1930) to Hohan Soken.

modifier: Nabe Matsumura, then Hohan Soken, who made the Matsumura Seito line public from 1952
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (created); Hohan Soken (standardised)
provenance: Preserved in the Matsumura family line to Nabe Matsumura and Hōhan Sōken (Matsumura Seito), and separately recorded by Kenwa Mabuni in Shitō-ryū as Matsumura no Passai; in Chibana's Kobayashi line the Passai Dai is likewise credited to Matsumura, with Itosu's as Passai Shō. The Matsumura recension, taught after the Itosu version. CORRECTION AND DEDUPLICATION. This row and 'Matsumura Bassai' are one label under two readings; keep one. The substantive problem is that the label covers two transmissions: (a) Matsumura Seito, Sokon Matsumura to Nabe Matsumura to Hohan Soken, who received two Passai, Dai and Sho; (b) Chibana's line and much of Shito-ryu, a form received from the Tawada family, which several writers hold was only later attributed to Matsumura, one calling it a publishing-era error. The two are described as sharing concepts but noticeably distinct in execution. Attribution to So

meaning: Uncertain. Commonly read as 'inside step-advancing'; the older Okinawan form Nifanchin suggests a Chinese source-name rather than a Japanese description
era: 19th century or earlier in Okinawa; Nidan and Sandan c. 1900
origin_person: Unknown. The kata is generally held to have entered Okinawa from Fuzhou; Sokon Matsumura is the most frequently named Okinawan candidate for the Shodan form, but this is tradition, not record
origin_place: Okinawa (Shuri and Tomari), from a Fuzhou source form known as Nifanchin
modifier: Anko Itosu, who is the leading candidate for dividing the material into three graded kata; alternative candidates named in the literature are Tokumine Pechin and Choki Motobu
modified_era: Division into Shodan/Nidan/Sandan c. 1900-1905, contemporaneous with Itosu's school-syllabus work; renamed Tekki by Funakoshi in 1935
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (transmitted); Karyu (Giko) Uku (transmitted); Tachimura no Peichin (transmitted); Anko Itosu (standardised); Tokumine Pechin (modified); Choki Motobu (modified); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed); Sokon Matsumura (standardised); Anko Itosu (created); Choki Motobu (standardised)
provenance: The oldest surviving written references to Naihanchi are in Choki Motobu's books of the 1920s-30s, where he states the kata was imported from China and was no longer practised there. Before Itosu introduced the Pinan series, Naihanchi was the first kata taught in both Shuri-te and Tomari-te, which is itself evidence of its antiquity. A separate Tomari line runs from Karyu (Giko) Uku to Kosaku Matsumora, and a separate Shuri line from Bushi Tachimura to Soko Kishimoto (Tachimura no Naihanchi). Motobu Choki made Naihanchi the core of his own practice and is the reason the kata carries a reputation as a complete fighting curriculum.

meaning: Conventionally glossed 'to storm/penetrate a fortress'; the name is probably a phonetic Okinawan rendering of a Chinese form-name and the gloss is a later back-formation
era: by the mid-19th century; no documentation earlier than the Matsumura/Oyadomari generation
origin_person: Unknown. Two competing traditions: a Chinese resident of Tomari (named in some accounts as Annan, the same castaway figure attached to Chinto and Chinte) who taught Kokan Oyadomari; and Sokon Matsumura, who is said to have assembled his Passai from material learned in China

modifier: Anko Itosu, who fixed the Passai Dai form used in the school syllabus and composed Passai Sho as a companion; Gichin Funakoshi, who renamed it Bassai for Japan

introduced_by: Annan (Chinese castaway resident in Tomari) (transmitted); Kokan Oyadomari (transmitted); Sokon Matsumura (transmitted); Kishin Teruya (transmitted); Kosaku Matsumora (transmitted); Anko Itosu (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (modified); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: Three named 19th-century streams survive: Matsumura no Passai (Sokon Matsumura, preserved through Nabe Matsumura and Hohan Soken in Matsumura Seito), Oyadomari/Tomari no Passai (Kokan Oyadomari, said to have learned it from a Chinese living in Tomari, transmitted onward through Kyan), and the Itosu line, which produced Passai Dai and Passai Sho and is the ancestor of the Shotokan Bassai Dai/Sho and the Shito-ryu forms. The Matsumura version is described as retaining a distinctly Chinese flavour, the Oyadomari version as more thoroughly 'Okinawanised'.

provenance: NEW, and deliberately flagged as ambiguous rather than given one identity. 'Passai Dai' denotes different kata in different lines. In Shito-ryu and general Okinawan usage it is Itosu's Passai, the same form Shotokan calls Bassai Dai. Matsumura Seito uses it for one of the two Passai received from Nabe Matsumura. Merging syllabus lists on this name without a line qualifier will fuse three different kata.

That is wrong for the Kobayashi case and misleading generally. In the Chibana/Kobayashi line 'Passai Sho' IS Itosu's Passai, the same form Shotokan calls Bassai Dai; Chibana used 'Passai Dai' for Tawada no Passai, reversing the expected sense of the names.
