modifier: Choyu Motobu (1857-1928), the last family holder, who transmitted it outside the family; Seikichi Uehara (1904-2004), who codified and publicised it as Motobu Udundi; Seitoku Higa, who preserved a version in the Bugeikan
modified_era: transmitted by Choyu Motobu c. 1920s; codified by Uehara from the 1940s-1970s onward
introduced_by: Choyu Motobu (transmitted); Seikichi Uehara (standardised); Seitoku Higa (standardised); Choyu Motobu (brought); Seitoku Higa (transmitted); Chosei Motobu (transmitted)
provenance: Motobu Udundi is presented as the private art of the Motobu royal branch family, passed to eldest sons only, and released to Seikichi Uehara by Choyu Motobu because no family successor was training. Mekata is its characteristic form: a dance-derived kata emphasising tuidi (seizing) and body-shifting rather than percussive striking.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, chapter on Motobu Udundi and Appendix C | roster entries: Choyu Motobu Q706389, Seikichi Uehara C00478, Motobu Chosei A0028

name: Motode Ichi and Ni
variants: Motode (five forms, per Cramer); Motode Ichi; Motode Ni; Motode Sanchin; Mutudi; Mutudī; Shuri Sanchin
meaning: 'Original hand' / 'root hand'; the base forms from which the system's applications are drawn
era: formalised in the 20th century; the tradition claims 17th-century palace roots
origin_person: DISPUTED between two Motobu brothers. Cramer states explicitly that the Motode kata and the twelve kumite forms were developed by Choki Motobu (1870-1944); the current database instead routes Motode through Choyu Motobu and Motobu Udundi
modifier: Choki Motobu, who taught Naihanchi Shodan and Nidan, Passai, Seisan, five Motode kata and twelve kumite forms as his complete curriculum; Seikichi Uehara for the Udundi line's version
modified_era: Choki Motobu's set fixed c. 1920s-1930s; Udundi codification from the 1940s onward
introduced_by: Choki Motobu (created); Choyu Motobu (transmitted); Seikichi Uehara (standardised); Chosei Motobu (transmitted); Choyu Motobu (brought)
provenance: Motobu Choki's son Chosei records that his father excluded from his teaching anything not practical in a martial sense, and that his instruction consisted of a small kata set plus paired forms. Cramer, drawing on that testimony, attributes the Motode kata and the kumite forms directly to Choki Motobu's own development.
sources: Motobu Chosei, testimony on his father's teaching, cited in the above | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, chapters on Motobu-ryu and Motobu Udundi

name: Oyadomari no Passai
meaning: Oyadomari's Passai
origin_person: Kokan Oyadomari (1827-1905) of Tomari, in a three-generation family transmission
modifier: Chotoku Kyan, whose recension is the one most widely practised
introduced_by: Kokan Oyadomari (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (transmitted); Kosaku Matsumora (transmitted)
provenance: Tomari family version passed to Kyan Chotoku and thence into Shorin-ryu, Isshin-ryu and Shito-ryu. Project edges also record the Chinese teachers Annan and Ason as inputs to Kokan Oyadomari, though both links are rated low confidence.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Rinkan
meaning: 'Between the trees' / 'in the grove'
era: 19th to early 20th century; first documented in the 20th century
origin_person: Unknown. Preserved in the Tomari line running Kosaku Matsumora to Kodatsu Iha to Seiyu Nakasone; no originator is recorded
modifier: Seiyu Nakasone (1893-1983), who transmitted it; Tokashiki Iken, who fixed the Gohakukai version and is the reason the kata survives at all
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (transmitted); Kodatsu Iha (transmitted); Seiyu Nakasone (transmitted); Tokashiki Iken (standardised); Seiyu Nakasone (brought); Seiyu Nakasone (created)
provenance: Tokashiki Iken, a student of Seiyu Nakasone and founder of the Gohakukai, is recorded as teaching Wankan, Wanshu Dai and Sho, Rohai, Kusanku, Chinto and Rinkan as the preserved Tomari-te set. Rinkan appears in no mainstream style syllabus and has no independent attestation outside this line.
sources: http://itosukai.blogspot.com/2020/12/wankan.html | https://wseku-karate.org/en/istoria-okinawa-karate/tomari-te/ | https://katastepbystep.com/karate-styles-tomari-te/ | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Rohai
variants: Itosu Rohai Shodan/Nidan/Sandan; Lohai; Matsumora Rohai (Tomari); Matsumura no Rohai; Meikyo; Meikyo (Shotokan reworking); No Hai; Rohai; Rohai Sho; Rōhai; Tomari Rohai
renamed_from: n/a for the Okinawan parent; see Meikyo
meaning: vision of a heron / heron sign
origin_person: Unknown; Tomari-te kata associated with Kosaku Matsumora
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
modifier: Anko Itosu (who split it into three); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed Meikyo)
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (brought); Anko Itosu (modified); Shoshin Nagamine (standardised); Anko Itosu (standardised); Hwang Kee (brought); Yun Kwae-byung (brought)
provenance: Tomari kata handed from Matsumora through Iha Kodatsu; Nagamine states he learned Tomari Rohai directly from Iha.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Tomari Bassai
meaning: Tomari version of Passai
origin_person: Unknown; the Tomari Passai tradition carried by Kishin Teruya and fixed by Kosaku Matsumora
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora; later Chotoku Kyan and Kodatsu Iha in their separate lines
modified_era: mid to late 19th century; Kyan and Iha recensions c. 1900-1930
introduced_by: Kishin Teruya (brought); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kokan Oyadomari (modified); Chotoku Kyan (transmitted); Kodatsu Iha (transmitted)
provenance: Nagamine states he learned Tomari Passai directly from Iha Kodatsu, one of the three principal heirs of Matsumora Kosaku.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Tomari Chinto
variants: Chinto; Chintō; Gankaku (Shotokan renaming of the Itosu line); Tomari no Chinto
meaning: Named after Chintō, said to be a shipwrecked Chinese sailor who taught in exchange for shelter; the name has no standard translation. Its significance lies in the one-legged crane stances and turning techniques, which led Funakoshi to rename the parallel Itosu version Gankaku ('crane on a rock').
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (brought); Shoshin Nagamine (standardised); Tatsuo Shimabuku (standardised)
provenance: The Chintō castaway story is folklore with Shuri (Matsumura) and Tomari (Matsumora/Gusukuma) tellings; the Tomari line ran Matsumora to Iha Kodatsu (Gohakukai) and Matsumora to Kyan, whose angled-embusen version passed into Matsubayashi-ryu, Seibukan, Shorinji-ryu and, via Shimabuku, Isshin-ryu. The Itosu/Shuri Chinto (Shotokan Gankaku) is a parallel line covered under Shuri-te. The Matsumora recension.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chint%C5%8D | https://www.karate4theheart.com/2020/04/the-kata-of-tomari-nerd-life-post.html | https://wseku-karate.org/en/istoria-okinawa-karate/tomari-te/

name: Tomari Kusanku
meaning: The Tomari transmission of Kusanku, named after the 18th-century Chinese envoy Kūsankū (Kong Sang Kun); distinct in pattern from the Chatan Yara and Itosu (Dai/Sho) versions. Significant as evidence that the Kusanku tradition entered Tomari independently of Shuri.
introduced_by: Kusanku (brought); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (brought); Tokashiki Iken (standardised)
provenance: Documented by Tokashiki Iken as one of the nine Gohakukai Tomari kata, transmitted Matsumora to Iha Kodatsu to Nakasone Seiyu; the attribution to the envoy Kusanku himself is traditional folklore. The mainstream Kusanku/Kanku family (Chatan Yara, Itosu, Kyan lines) is covered under Shuri-te.
sources: https://www.karate4theheart.com/2020/04/the-kata-of-tomari-nerd-life-post.html | https://iogkfmadrid.wordpress.com/2010/02/09/donde-goju-ryu-y-tomari-te-se-encuentran-tokashiki-iken-y-el-gohakukai/

name: Tomari Naihanchi
variants: Matsumora no Naihanchi; Naifanchi (Tomari-di); Naifanchi I-III (Gohakukai); Tomari no Naifanchi
meaning: See Naihanchi
era: early 19th century in Tomari; taught to Matsumora in the 1830s-40s
origin_person: Unknown. The named Tomari transmitter is Karyu (Giko) Uku (1800-1850), who taught the three Naihanchi as the foundation of the Tomari curriculum
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; ultimate source Chinese, via Fuzhou
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora, who fixed the Tomari form; Kodatsu Iha and Seiyu Nakasone transmitted it onward; Tokashiki Iken standardised the Gohakukai version
modified_era: Matsumora's form fixed mid-to-late 19th century; Gohakukai standardisation from the 1970s
introduced_by: Karyu (Giko) Uku (transmitted); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (transmitted); Seiyu Nakasone (transmitted); Tokashiki Iken (standardised); Karyu Uku (brought)
provenance: Nagamine records directly that Matsumora Kosaku's first teacher was Uku Giko (1800-1850), in whose courtyard he trained for three years and from whom he learned 'the three kata known in Tomari as Naihanchi'. This is one of the firmest named transmissions in the whole Tomari corpus and is a first-hand-derived account, not folklore.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%8Dsaku_Matsumora | https://www.karate4theheart.com/2020/04/the-kata-of-tomari-nerd-life-post.html | https://wseku-karate.org/en/istoria-okinawa-karate/tomari-te/

name: Tomari Passai
variants: Bassai; Matsumora no Passai; Oyadomari no Passai; Passai; Tomari Bassai; Tomari no Passai
meaning: See Passai
era: early-to-mid 19th century; taught to Matsumora in the 1840s
origin_person: Unknown. The named Tomari transmitter is Kishin Teruya (1804-1864), for whom Passai and Wanshu were the favourite kata; a parallel Tomari line runs through Kokan Oyadomari, said to have learned Passai from a Chinese resident of Tomari
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora and Kokan Oyadomari, who fixed the two Tomari shapes; Chotoku Kyan, who carried the Oyadomari form into the Shorin lines
modified_era: Tomari forms fixed mid-to-late 19th century; Kyan's version c. 1900-1930
introduced_by: Kishin Teruya (transmitted); Kokan Oyadomari (transmitted); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (modified); Kishin Teruya (brought); Kokan Oyadomari (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (brought)
provenance: Nagamine records that under Teruya Kishin the young Matsumora spent 'more than three years being grounded in Passai and Wanshu, the favorite kata of his teacher', and that Teruya later revealed the bunkai to him at the family tomb near Ameku. Separately, Oyadomari no Passai is transmitted through the Oyadomari family to Kyan and is the direct ancestor of the Matsubayashi and Seibukan versions.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kokan_Oyadomari | https://www.ikigaiway.com/making-sense-of-passai-an-exploration-of-origin-and-style/ | https://www.karate4theheart.com/2020/04/the-kata-of-tomari-nerd-life-post.html

name: Tomari Rohai
variants: Matsumora Rohai; Matsumora no Rohai; Meikyo (Shotokan); Ro Hai (Tang Soo Do); Rohai; Rohai Shodan / Nidan / Sandan (Itosu); Rōhai
meaning: 'Vision of a crane' / 'heron sign'; the crane imagery refers to the one-legged sagi-ashi-dachi postures
origin_person: Kosaku Matsumora is named in the literature as the presumed inventor, which is why the form is called Matsumora Rohai; the attribution is traditional, not documented
modifier: Anko Itosu, who derived Rohai Shodan, Nidan and Sandan from this form for the school syllabus; Kodatsu Iha and Shoshin Nagamine preserved the Tomari original; Funakoshi's Meikyo derives from the Itosu branch
modified_era: Itosu's three-kata division c. 1900-1907; Funakoshi's Meikyo renamed 1935 and reworked in Shotokan in the late 1930s-40s
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (created); Anko Itosu (modified); Kodatsu Iha (transmitted); Shoshin Nagamine (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (brought)
provenance: Nagamine records learning Tomari Rohai (with Tomari Passai, Chinto, Wankan and Wanshu) directly from Kodatsu Iha, giving a clean four-step chain Matsumora to Iha to Nagamine. Itosu's three Rohai are the branch from which Shotokan's Meikyo descends, and who combined the three into the single Shotokan form is not recorded.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C5%8Dhai | https://www.historyoffighting.com/the-blog/the-history-of-meikyo | https://ikku.org/the-rohai-kata-series/

name: Tomari Seisan
era: documented 1930 in Kenpo Gaisetsu; transmission 19th century
origin_person: Unknown; Chinese source form. Kinjo Hiroshi suspects it may be the 'cross-over' Okinawan representation of old Chinese quanfa, possibly the Aragaki or Kume version.
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora or Kokan Oyadomari at the head of the chain (accounts differ); Kodatsu Iha; Chojo Oshiro; Hiroshi Kinjo
provenance: NEW RECORD. Entered so the one documented Okinawan Seisan chain is visible in the data. The 1930 'Kenpo Gaisetsu' of Miki Nisaburo and Takada Mizuho records an 'Oshiro Seisan', transmitted (per Joe Swift reporting Kinjo Hiroshi) Matsumora Kosaku to Iha Kodatsu (1873-1928) to Oshiro Chojo (1887-1935); McCarthy gives the same chain with Oyadomari Kokan at the head instead of Matsumora. Oshiro was Kinjo Hiroshi's teacher, and Kinjo passed both this and a 'Matsumura Seisan' to McCarthy.

name: Wando
meaning: Uncertain; the 'Wan' element links it to Wanshu and Wankan as a name group, and may point back to the Wang Ji tradition
origin_person: Unknown. Grouped in the Tomari tradition with Wanshu and Wankan as a set of three sharing a common lineage, which by implication routes it to the same 1683 Wang Ji tradition, but nothing is documented
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora is the earliest named holder; the kata is now rare and survives mainly in Gohakukai and a few Tomari-te preservation lines
modified_era: 19th century; documented only in 20th-century preservation efforts
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (transmitted); Kodatsu Iha (transmitted); Tokashiki Iken (standardised); Shogo Kuniba (standardised); Kosaku Matsumora (brought)
provenance: Sources treat Wankan, Wanshu and Wandau/Wando as a Tomari triad of common origin. Wando is the least-transmitted of the three and is close to extinct outside specialist preservation groups.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wankan | http://itosukai.blogspot.com/2020/12/wankan.html | https://www.karate4theheart.com/2020/04/the-kata-of-tomari-nerd-life-post.html | Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C

name: Wanduan
meaning: uncertain
origin_person: Unknown; same obscure Tomari group as Wando and Wankan
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (transmitted); Shogo Kuniba (standardised)
provenance: Same Tomari cluster as Wando; survives almost entirely through tournament transmission.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List [membership and spelling uncertain]

name: Wankan
variants: Hito (Genseiryu); Matsukaze; Matsukaze (Shito-ryu); Ohan (unrelated); Okan; Wankan (Shotokan); Wankan (Shotokan, distinct short form); Wankuan; Ōkan
meaning: 'King's crown' / 'crown of a king'
origin_person: Unknown. Kosaku Matsumora is the earliest identifiable holder; he most probably had it from one of his two teachers, Karyu (Giko) Uku or Kishin Teruya
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora fixed the Tomari form; Kodatsu Iha and Seiyu Nakasone transmitted it; Shoshin Nagamine standardised the Matsubayashi version; Kenwa Mabuni renamed it Matsukaze in Shito-ryu; a separate short Shotokan Wankan is attributed to Gigo Funakoshi
modified_era: Tomari form fixed mid-to-late 19th century; Matsubayashi version from 1947; Shotokan version late 1930s-1940s
introduced_by: Karyu (Giko) Uku (transmitted); Kishin Teruya (transmitted); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (transmitted); Seiyu Nakasone (transmitted); Shoshin Nagamine (standardised); Kenwa Mabuni (renamed); Tokashiki Iken (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (brought); Gigo Funakoshi (modified)
provenance: Wankan originated in Tomari alongside Wanshu and Wandau (Wando), the three sharing a common lineage. Transmission ran Matsumora to Kodatsu Iha (1873-1928), and from Iha to both Shoshin Nagamine and Seiyu Nakasone; Nakasone taught Tokashiki Iken, founder of the Gohakukai, who preserved Wankan with Wanshu Dai and Sho, Rohai, Kusanku, Chinto and Rinkan.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wankan | http://itosukai.blogspot.com/2020/12/wankan.html | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%8Dsaku_Matsumora

name: Wanshu
variants: Anshu; Empi; Empi / Enpi (Shotokan); Enpi; Enpi (Shotokan); Kyan no Wansu; Matsumora no Wanshu; Wanshū Dai; Wanshū Shō; Wansu; Wansū; Yun Bi (Tang Soo Do)
meaning: named after the envoy Wang Ji
era: folklore places the source visit in 1683; documented transmission 19th century
origin_person: Wang Ji (Wanshu), Qing envoy to Ryukyu, per folklore
modifier: Chotoku Kyan (Shorin recension); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed Enpi, 1936)
modified_era: late 19th to early 20th century; Shotokan Enpi fixed 1936
introduced_by: Wang Ji (transmitted); Kishin Teruya (brought); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (modified); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed); Maeda Pechin (brought); Chotoku Kyan (brought); Wang Ji (created); Kishin Teruya (transmitted); Maeda Pechin (transmitted)
provenance: Tomari transmission from Teruya Kishin to Matsumora Kosaku; Kyan's version passed into Shorin and Isshin lines. Nagamine records the renaming to Enpi.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Wansu
variants: Empi / Enpi (燕飛); Wang Shu; Wanshū; Wansū
meaning: Traditionally named after Wang Ji (Wanshū), a Chinese sappūshi envoy said to have visited Tomari in 1683 (folklore); Funakoshi's Empi (燕飛) means 'flight of the swallow', after its darting rising-and-dropping movement.
era: folklore places the source visit in 1683; kata documented from the 19th century
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: A Tomari-te kata in origin, listed here for its Shuri-line transmission: Kyan learned it in Tomari (Maeda Pēchin's line) and spread it to Seibukan, Matsubayashi-ryū and Isshin-ryū, while Itosu's students carried a version to Japan, where Funakoshi renamed it Empi in the mid-1930s. The Wang Ji story is folklore; the Tomari mainline is covered under the Tomari-te area. Same kata as Wanshu under the Okinawan spelling.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wansh%C5%AB | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C5%8Dtoku_Kyan

name: Kanchin
meaning: 'Kanbun's battles', from Uechi Kanbun
introduced_by: Kanei Uechi (created)
provenance: Seventh kata, the last of Kanei Uechi's additions and the immediate preparation for Sanseiryu. Named to honour his father Kanbun.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uechi-Ry%C5%AB | https://www.uechiryu-europe.org/en/les-katas-du-uechi-ryu/ | https://w.traditionaluechi-ryu.com/eng/kata2.html

name: Kanshiwa
variants: Kan Shi Wa; Kanshabu; Kanshabu (early name)
meaning: 'Kan' from Uechi Kanbun, 'Shiwa' from Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe)
introduced_by: Kanei Uechi (created); Saburo Uehara (created); Kanei Uechi (renamed)
provenance: First of the five bridging kata inserted between Sanchin and Seisan when Uechi Kanei opened the curriculum to large postwar classes. Originally named Kanshabu (Kan from Kanbun, Shabu from 'Shu Shabu'), renamed Kanshiwa in 1970 when the Uechi-ryu Karate-do Kyokai standardised kata names.
sources: https://www.uechiryu-europe.org/en/les-katas-du-uechi-ryu/ | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uechi-Ry%C5%AB | https://w.traditionaluechi-ryu.com/eng/kata2.html | https://uechi-ryu.com/uechi-kanei/

name: Kanshu
variants: Dai Ni Seisan; Daini Seisan; Daini Seisan (second Seisan, early name); Kanshiu; Kanshiwa (distinct); Kansu
meaning: 'Kan' from Uechi Kanbun, 'Shu' from Shu Shiwa (Zhou 周)
modified_era: 1970 renaming; further adjusted within Konan-ryu after 1978
introduced_by: Seiki Itokazu (created); Kanei Uechi (standardised); Kanei Uechi (renamed)
provenance: Third kata of the Uechi order. Created under the name Daini Seisan ('Second Seisan') because it recombines Seisan material at a lower level; renamed Kanshu in 1970 in the same naming reform that produced Kanshiwa. Itokazu Seiki (1915-2006) later left the Uechi family organisation in 1978 and, with Kinjo Takashi, founded Konan-ryu, which retains the kata.
sources: https://www.uechiryu-europe.org/en/les-katas-du-uechi-ryu/ | https://w.traditionaluechi-ryu.com/eng/kata2.html | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uechi-Ry%C5%AB | https://forums.uechi-ryu.com/viewtopic.php?t=15919

name: Ryuko
meaning: 'Dragon and Tiger', from the dragon-tiger-crane triad of Pangai-noon
era: developed late 1990s to c. 2005; taught publicly from the mid-2000s
origin_person: committee of senior instructors of the Okinawa Karate-do Kyokai (Okikukai / Shohei-ryu)
modified_era: c. 2005, when the sequence was fixed for grading
introduced_by: Okinawa Karate-do Kyokai (Okikukai) senior board (created); Tsutomu Nakahodo (created); Ryuko Tomoyose (transmitted)
provenance: Ninth kata of the Okikukai branch, created after the 1991 split from the Uechi family soke line. Composed by a committee rather than one man, over a period reported as at least seven years. Longer than Sanseiryu and positioned as the senior form, explicitly analogous to Suparinpei in Goju-ryu and Kusanku in Shorin-ryu.
sources: https://forums.uechi-ryu.com/viewtopic.php?t=21403 | https://forums.uechi-ryu.com/viewtopic.php?t=15892 | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uechi-Ry%C5%AB | https://www.stoughtondojo.com/shohei-uechi/urkd.html

name: Sanchin (Uechi)
meaning: 'Three battles' or 'three conflicts'
era: learned in Fujian c. 1897-1907; taught in Japan from 1926 and on Okinawa from 1947
modified_era: c. 1947-1970, when the Uechi curriculum was formalised at the Futenma dojo
introduced_by: Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe) (transmitted); Kanbun Uechi (brought); Kanei Uechi (standardised)
provenance: Pangai-noon Sanchin, distinct from the Higaonna/Miyagi Naha-te Sanchin already in the database. Open-hand throughout (nukite rather than the Goju closed fist), no turns in the classical Uechi version, and performed with a different breathing pattern. Kanbun Uechi learned it from Zhou Zihe in Fuzhou and taught it in Wakayama from 1926; Kanei Uechi fixed the Okinawan performance standard after 1947.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanbun_Uechi | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uechi-Ry%C5%AB | https://www.uechiryu-europe.org/en/les-katas-du-uechi-ryu/

name: Sanseiryu
meaning: thirty-six
era: Qing-era China; learned by Kanbun Uechi c. 1897-1907
origin_person: Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe, 1874-1926), who taught it to Kanbun Uechi; ultimate creator unknown
modifier: Kanei Uechi, who formalised the Uechi-ryu syllabus
introduced_by: Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe) (transmitted); Kanbun Uechi (brought); Kanei Uechi (standardised)
provenance: One of the three kata Kanbun Uechi brought from Fujian; distinct from the Goju Sanseiru despite the shared numeral.
sources: WKF Competition Rules, Appendix: Official Kata List

name: Seichin
variants: Seichin (Uechi); Seichin (also glossed 'ten battles' or as a Sanchin-Seisan blend); Seichin no Kata
meaning: 'Ten battles', ten being the number of core techniques drilled
modified_era: c. 1970 standardisation of the Uechi syllabus
introduced_by: Saburo Uehara (created); Kanei Uechi (standardised)
provenance: Fourth kata, bridging Kanshu and Seisan. Uehara Saburo (1900-1965) was a direct student of Uechi Kanbun in Wakayama and one of the senior figures consulted when Kanei built the expanded syllabus.
sources: https://uechi-ryu.com/saburo-uehara/ | https://www.uechiryu-europe.org/en/les-katas-du-uechi-ryu/ | https://w.traditionaluechi-ryu.com/eng/kata2.html | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uechi-Ry%C5%AB

name: Seiryu
meaning: 'Sixteen', from the number of techniques
introduced_by: Kanei Uechi (created)
provenance: Sixth kata, placed after Seisan. Created at the Futenma dojo as part of Kanei Uechi's postwar expansion of the three-kata Pangai-noon syllabus into eight.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uechi-Ry%C5%AB | https://www.uechiryu-europe.org/en/les-katas-du-uechi-ryu/ | https://w.traditionaluechi-ryu.com/eng/kata2.html

name: Seisan (Uechi)
meaning: 'Thirteen'

name: Shinshu
meaning: 'Shin' from Shinki, 'Shu' from Shubukai
introduced_by: Satoru Shinki (created)
provenance: Created for the Uechi-ryu Karate-do Shubukai as a fusion of Okinawan Ti material with Pangai-noon technique. Distinguished by a reversed watari-uke and an explicitly anticipatory strategy, which is atypical of the classical Uechi forms.
sources: https://www.traditionaluechi-ryu.com/eng/modernkata.html | https://w.traditionaluechi-ryu.com/eng/kata2.html
